items.name: dot-pattern
items.title: DotPattern
items.lead: Adds a quiet field of dots behind a composition.

docs.lead: Adds a quiet field of dots behind a composition.
docs.name: DotPattern
docs.summary: A decorative dot-grid layer for canvas grounds — the texture behind the Creative Editor stage and the Library's business-card previews. It fills its container absolutely and paints evenly spaced circular dots, nothing else: no ground of its own, no edge, no pointer target. Geometry defaults transcribe the shipped Paper shader recipe (2px dots on a 16px pitch); the dot ink is border-subtle carried as currentColor, so className retints it with any ink utility, and the container keeps its own background showing through between the dots.

anatomy.notes: The only node — an aria-hidden SVG, absolutely inset to the container's box, pointer-events none. It holds a <pattern> tile of one centred circle per gap×gap cell and a full-size <rect> painted with it. The CONTAINER is the caller's: position relative, its own background (bg-sunken in both shipped usages) and any clipping radius belong there, never here.

docs.composition:
DotPattern └─ (no children — gap and dotSize shape the tile, className carries colour)
{/* content stacks above in normal flow — no z-index needed */} …
// Denser, stronger, retinted — geometry via props, colour via className:

gap.notes: Pitch between dot centres, px, both axes. A plain number rather than a spacing token on purpose — density is geometry, not spacing semantics (sheet, Geometry). The tile starts at the container's top-left, so the first dot centre sits at (gap/2, gap/2) and edges clip mid-dot instead of the grid re-centring on resize.

dotSize.notes: Dot diameter, px. The default is the shader's `size: 1` read as a radius — @paper-design/shaders' dot-grid GLSL treats u_dotSize as the distance from cell centre to dot edge — so the shipped look is 2px diameter (sheet, Gaps § Dot size).

className.notes: Colour lives here, in tokens. The dots ride on currentColor with text-edge-subtle as the default ink, so `text-edge-default` is the strong opt-in and any ink utility retints. A background on the layer itself is a `bg-*` utility the same way — but the shipped composition paints the CONTAINER instead, which is what keeps one pattern working over any surface token.

do: Give the container position: relative, its own background, and the clipping radius — the layer paints dots and nothing else.
Put content after the pattern in source order; it stacks above without z-index because the layer comes first.
Retint with an ink utility in className (text-edge-default when the grid must read at a glance); the default border-subtle grain is deliberately near-invisible.
Change density with gap and weight with dotSize — 8/16/24 and 1/2/4 are the drawn range on the sheet.
dont: Do not make the grid carry information. It measures 1.21:1 against bg-sunken by design — anything that must be read sits on the content above it.
Do not wrap it in a positioned shim to place it — the component is already absolute inset 0; position the CONTAINER.
Do not reach for a raw hex to retint it. The two inks the design draws are border-subtle and border-default; a third colour is a design question for the sheet, not a call-site invention.
Do not expect pointer events on it — the layer is pointer-events none so canvas interactions land on the container and content.

a11y.role: none — an aria-hidden SVG. The attribute sits AFTER the prop spread, so it is contract rather than default: a texture never names anything, which is the difference from Skeleton's overridable default.
a11y.name: None, ever.
a11y.focus: Never focusable and never a pointer target (pointer-events: none). Nothing about the layer participates in interaction.

contrastPairs.why: The default dot ink against the canvas ground both shipped usages use — 1.21:1 light, 1.12:1 dark (#302D2A on the #383531 sunken fill, 2026-11-03; the strong opt-in is 1.22:1 there), deliberately below any floor and declared decorative on the sheet (Gaps § Contrast). The grid is grain, not information; nothing may depend on seeing it. Declared rather than omitted so the number stays measured in both schemes.
The strong opt-in ink (sheet, Colour). Still decorative — stronger only so the grid reads at a glance where the canvas metaphor wants it, never because something depends on it.

forwarding.ref: Goes to the svg — the only node, not a form control, so the §5 default applies.
forwarding.className: Lands on the svg and merges last: text-* utilities displace the default ink, bg-* adds a layer ground, and pointer-events/position defaults are displaceable the same way.
forwarding.rest: Native SVG props go to the svg. `children` is typed out — the tile is generated from gap and dotSize, and arbitrary children inside the <svg> would silently not be the pattern. `aria-hidden` is set after the spread and cannot be overridden.

docs.motion: None. The shader's sizeRange and opacityRange randomisers were 0 in both shipped usages; the grid is static, so prefers-reduced-motion has nothing to remove (sheet, Behaviour § Motion).
needsDesign: Only square grids are drawn: the shader exposes gapX/gapY separately but both usages set them equal, so the component ships one `gap`. An anisotropic grid is a new sheet row before it is a prop.
DotGrid's square and diamond dot shapes, stroke, and the size/opacity randomisers are not carried over — both shipped usages draw plain circles (sheet, Gaps § Shader extras).
knownGaps: No geometry spec (design/paper/specs/) exists for this item, deliberately: the geometry laws measure container/child insets and gaps from world coordinates, and a tile pitch has neither a padding box nor children to measure. The pattern numbers the sheet fixes (gap 16, dot 2, first centre at gap/2) are asserted directly in dot-pattern.browser.test.tsx instead.

The dot ink defaults through a Tailwind utility (text-edge-subtle), not a component CSS variable — so retinting is a className, which is the system's idiom, but there is no --ui-dot-pattern-* override surface below it. If a brand needs to move the default without touching call sites, that is the moment to add one.

The layer needs a positioned ancestor. Inside a static container, absolute inset-0 resolves against the nearest positioned ancestor instead — the grid silently paints somewhere else. The browser test pins the intended composition; the doc cannot stop a static container.

Sub-pixel dot edges are the browser's to rasterise. A 2px circle on a 16px pitch renders crisply at 1x and 2x, but a fractional dotSize lands on antialiasing — the sheet only draws integer diameters (1, 2, 4).

changes.summary: Public library pages follow the manifest and typed documentation, with article-inspired copy and no changing library totals. Public leads and categories feed generated HTML references, Markdown twins, gallery and search entries, agent indexes and registry routes. The optional NetworkCanvas renderer now has its own typed reference. New freshness, source-boundary, route/link and browser checks keep the public reader in step. Interactive specimens are a featured subset; hosting and the remaining release gates stay open.

DotPattern: a decorative dot-grid layer for canvas grounds — the texture behind the Creative Editor stage and the Library's business-card previews, both drawn in Paper with the @paper-design/shaders DotGrid shader (size 1, gapX = gapY = 16, circle, colorFill #DAD4CE, colorBack transparent, over bg-sunken). One aria-hidden SVG, absolute inset-0, pointer-events none: a <pattern> tile of one centred circle per gap×gap cell and a full-size rect. Geometry is two plain-number props (gap 16, dotSize 2 — the shader's size is a RADIUS in its GLSL, so the shipped look is a 2px diameter; recorded on the sheet's Gaps section) and colour is className through currentColor, defaulting to text-edge-subtle — the first non-ink text-colour utility in the library; the browser test pins the tailwind-merge override actually winning. The library renders SVG rather than the WebGL shader deliberately: identical geometry, no runtime dependency, crisp at any DPR, printable — also recorded on the sheet, along with the observation that Paper's exports do not rasterise shader nodes, so the sheet's provenance is the shader's parameter record (get_jsx), not pixels. No geometry spec (specs/) exists for this item on purpose: the ADR 0019 laws measure container/child insets and a tile pitch has neither, so the pattern numbers are asserted in dot-pattern.browser.test.tsx instead. Both dot inks are declared decorative contrast pairs (border-subtle on bg-sunken is 1.21:1 light / 1.53:1 dark by design, measured by check:contrast — the grid is grain, not information; the doc's dont list forbids making it load-bearing). aria-hidden sits AFTER the prop spread — contract, not Skeleton's overridable default — because a texture never names anything.

items.name: drawer
items.title: Drawer
items.lead: Brings a panel up from the bottom, ready to dismiss with a drag.

docs.lead: Brings a panel up from the bottom, ready to dismiss with a drag.
docs.name: Drawer
docs.summary: A panel that comes up from the bottom and is dismissed by dragging it down. Distinct from Sheet, and the distinction is the GESTURE rather than the geometry (CONVENTIONS §7a): a Sheet is anchored to a side edge and dismissed by scrim or Escape, while a Drawer carries a handle and follows the finger. Base UI supplies the focus trap and scroll lock; the drag is ours, with no drag library in the dependency list.

anatomy.notes: The control that opens it. Pass your own element via `render` — never wrapped.
The backdrop, --ui-scrim. The sheet drew this as --ui-bg-emphasis-active, an opaque surface role with no alpha; corrected in Paper.
The drawer. Inset 4px on three sides, radius-lg on all four corners, bg-base with a 1px edge and shadow-md. Capped at 80% of the viewport.
A real <button> covering the full 32px header band. Drag it to dismiss; tap it to dismiss without dragging.
The 8px pill at 30% width, bg-sunken. Decorative — the button around it is the control.

The 48px chrome band the sheet draws on the desktop panel: `p-sm` uniform, justify-between, holding chromeControls — a fill with no edge is page chrome, not a Button (§7b). Sheet.Header's values exactly; both were drawn on this artboard. Optional, and an ADDITION to the handle rather than a replacement for it — see needsDesign.
body-lg at bold weight, clamped to one line. Becomes nothing automatically — the panel's `label` is the accessible name.
p-lg, gap-sm. Scrolls when the drawer hits its cap.
p-lg, gap-sm, and a COLUMN — buttons stack full width, unlike Modal's row.

docs.composition:
Drawer                     isOpen? / defaultIsOpen? / onOpenChange? / isDismissable?
├─ Drawer.Trigger          render={<Button>…</Button>}
└─ Drawer.Panel            label (required) / handleLabel? / container? / initialFocus? / finalFocus?
   ├─ (drag handle)        drawn by Panel, not composed
   ├─ Drawer.Header?        the 48px chrome band — chromeControls, never a Title
   │  └─ Drawer.Close       render={<button className={chromeControl()} …/>}
   ├─ Drawer.Title?
   ├─ Drawer.Body
   │  └─ <your content>    Inputs, a form, anything
   └─ Drawer.Footer
      ├─ <primary action>  <Button isFullWidth shape="full">
      └─ Drawer.Close      render={<Button variant="secondary" isFullWidth shape="full">Cancel</Button>}

label.notes: On Panel. A dialog with no accessible name is announced as 'dialog' and nothing else. Drawer.Title is visible content and is not wired to it automatically — use the same words in both.

handleLabel.notes: The handle is a real button as well as a drag target, so it needs a name. Rename it when 'Close' would be ambiguous on the screen.

Panel.initialFocus.notes: Where focus lands when the drawer opens. The default is the first tabbable element inside it, which is the drag handle, and that handle is also a close button. Pass the ref of the control the drawer exists for. A function is called at open time; returning null, or a ref that is still empty, keeps the default rather than dropping focus. Restated as DrawerFocusTarget, the same shape as Sheet's SheetFocusTarget, and deliberately not Base UI's, whose `false` would leave focus behind the scrim.

Panel.finalFocus.notes: Where focus goes when the drawer closes. The default is the trigger, or whatever was focused before it opened. Set it when that element will be gone. Same fallback rule as initialFocus.

isOpen.notes: Controlled. Omit and the drawer owns it.

onOpenChange.notes: One callback for both directions (§1). Narrowed from Base UI's signature so no third-party type reaches ours.

isDismissable.notes: Escape and scrim-tap. It does NOT disable the drag: the handle is the drawer's defining affordance, and a drawer you can grab but not move is broken furniture. Use a Modal if the decision genuinely cannot be deferred.

Panel.snapPoints.notes: Resting heights as fractions of the viewport, ASCENDING — [0.5, 0.9]. Omit for one content-sized height. Rendered in `dvh` rather than `vh`, because on mobile `vh` is the viewport with the browser chrome hidden, so a 0.5 drawer is not half of what anyone can see. An empty array falls back rather than rendering a zero-height panel.

Panel.snapPoint.notes: Controlled detent, as an INDEX into snapPoints — not the fraction.

Panel.onSnapPointChange.notes: One callback for every path — drag, tap and controlled update all go through it (§1).

container.notes: Where the panel is portalled. Theme tokens are INHERITED custom properties, so a panel in the body leaves any brand scope on a wrapper and paints theme zero. See sheet.doc.ts for why it is a prop rather than automatic.

do: Give every drawer a label, and repeat it as a Drawer.Title when the design shows a heading.
Stack footer actions full width — that is what the sheet draws, and the bottom of the screen is where a thumb lands.
Reach for a Drawer when the content is a quick, deferrable task on a phone; reach for a Sheet when it is navigation.
dont: Do not use a Drawer where a Sheet belongs. They are not `side` variants of one component: a Drawer's contract is a gesture, and a Sheet has no handle, no velocity threshold and no body that follows the finger.
Do not put a long scrolling list in the body and expect the drag to work from anywhere — the handle is the drag target, deliberately, so a scroll inside the body never fights the gesture.

Do not rely on the drag alone. Without snapPoints a tap on the handle closes it; with them a tap STEPS UP and wraps from the tallest back to the shortest, so both directions stay reachable, and dismissal moves to the scrim and Escape.
Do not import Base UI types into your own props — `check:boundaries` fails the build (ADR 0002).

a11y.role: dialog, modal (from Base UI). The page behind is inert and does not scroll while open.
a11y.name: The `label` prop, as aria-label.

keyboard.does: Opens from the trigger, and closes from the handle — it is a real button, so both are native.
Closes when isDismissable, and RESTORES FOCUS to the trigger. Asserted in Chromium.
Cycles within the panel only; focus cannot reach the page behind.

a11y.focus: Focus moves into the panel on open and returns to the trigger on close, both from the behaviour layer and both asserted in Chromium. `initialFocus` and `finalFocus` on the Panel move either end deliberately; both are asserted against the default they replace.
a11y.pointer: The drag is never the only way. SC 2.5.7 (Dragging Movements) requires a single-pointer alternative to EVERY dragging movement, and detents give the drag three of them — expand, collapse, dismiss. Tapping the handle steps up and wraps from the tallest back to the shortest, covering expand and collapse; the scrim and Escape cover dismissal. A tap that sometimes expanded and sometimes threw the drawer away would be worse than either.
a11y.target: The handle button is the full 32px header band, not the 8px bar inside it — the bar alone would be an 8px target against SC 2.5.8's 24px floor.

contrastPairs.role: the title and content on the panel

contrastPairs.why: The handle bar is a grip, not a control boundary — the 32px button around it is the control, and its focus ring is what has to be visible. Holding the bar itself to 3:1 would make it a dark slab across the top of every drawer.
contrastPairs.role: the handle bar against the panel

needsDesign: Does the DESKTOP form drop the drag handle? "Drawer Desktop" draws the chrome band and no handle, where both mobile panels draw a handle and no band — but the handle is the drag affordance AND the single-pointer alternative SC 2.5.7 requires of every dragging movement, so it cannot simply be conditioned on width. Drawer.Header ships as an ADDITION rather than a replacement until this is answered: compose both today, and the panel has a 32px handle above a 48px band.
The 80% height cap applies only WITHOUT snapPoints; with them the tallest detent is the cap. The half-open sheet draws 0.5, and the tall detent is still derived.
knownGaps: Detents are OPT-IN via snapPoints. Without them the drawer keeps exactly its old behaviour — one content-sized height, a drag that only goes down, and a handle tap that closes.

Drag works from the HANDLE only, not the whole panel. Dragging from anywhere means arbitrating with scroll position inside the body on every pointer move; the handle is unambiguous, and it is the affordance the sheet draws.

The 80% height cap is DERIVED and applies only without snapPoints; with them the tallest detent is the cap, or a 0.9 snap point would be silently truncated to 0.8. The half-open sheet (J88-0) draws the 0.5 detent; the taller one is still a demo height.
The scrim does not fade with the drag. It fades on open and close only; tying its opacity to the offset is a refinement, not a contract.

CLOSED 2026-08-25: the sheet's two SELECT fields (Occupation, Visibility) are real Selects in the story now. They were Inputs while Select did not exist — Multiselect being the wrong shape for a single value — and the stand-in outlived the reason for it by longer than it should have.

Drawer.Header SHIPPED 2026-08-25 — the 48px chrome band this component's own sheet draws and had never had. "Drawer Desktop" opens with it: back and forward chrome controls at the leading edge, a close at the trailing one, `p-sm` uniform so 8 + 32 + 8 = 48 agrees with the pinned height. Sheet.Header's values exactly, which is unsurprising — both were drawn on this artboard. It does NOT carry Sheet.Header's scrolled hairline: this sheet draws no scrolled state, and inventing one is how a drawing stops being a contract.
No visual-regression baseline — the matrix renders inline and a Drawer portals to document.body, the same exclusion Modal, Popover and Sheet have.
docs.motion: Two tiers, and this is the only component in the library with the second. CSS: the scrim fades and the panel translates from `translate-y-full` through `data-[starting-style]`/`data-[ending-style]`, both `transition-[translate,opacity]` at --ui-duration-base with --ui-ease-out. JavaScript: while a finger is down the transition is switched off (`transition-none`) and the panel's `translate` is written directly from pointer state, so it tracks the finger exactly instead of lagging a frame behind it. No motion runtime is involved. The drag deliberately does not consult prefers-reduced-motion — the panel is being moved BY the user, not animated at them; the token-layer collapse still governs the enter, exit and snap-back.

contrast.role: the title and content on the panel
the handle bar against the panel

changes.summary: Public library pages follow the manifest and typed documentation, with article-inspired copy and no changing library totals. Public leads and categories feed generated HTML references, Markdown twins, gallery and search entries, agent indexes and registry routes. The optional NetworkCanvas renderer now has its own typed reference. New freshness, source-boundary, route/link and browser checks keep the public reader in step. Interactive specimens are a featured subset; hosting and the remaining release gates stay open.

Modal.Surface and Drawer.Panel declare `initialFocus` and `finalFocus`, the same props #28 gave Sheet.Panel, with the same semantics. Both forwarded `rest` to Base UI's Dialog.Popup untyped, so the props already reached the behaviour layer by accident. They were undeclared, and a rename upstream would have broken them silently. Each takes a ref or a function returning the element. A function returning null, or a ref still empty, keeps the default instead of dropping focus. Base UI's boolean and interaction-type forms are not offered, because `false` would leave focus behind the scrim. The types are restated locally as `ModalFocusTarget` and `DrawerFocusTarget` rather than shared from a lib item, because the components ship as independent source and every other behaviour-layer shape in these files (DismissDetails, the forBaseUI shim) is restated per file. check:boundaries stays green. For a Drawer the default matters more than it looks: the first tabbable element is the drag handle, which is also a close button. The browser tests put two buttons ahead of the target and assert focus lands on it and returns to a named element on Escape, in both forms, against a control case proving the defaults. Removing the mapping fails all eight.

migration.manual: A caller passing `initialFocus`/`finalFocus` through the untyped spread keeps working with a ref or a function returning an element. A boolean, or a function taking Base UI's interaction type, no longer type-checks; pass a ref or `() => element` instead.

changes.summary: The Drawer sheet draws a 48px chrome band this component does not have, recorded as a known gap. "Drawer Desktop" opens with a row of back and forward chrome controls at the leading edge and a close at the trailing one, p-sm, sitting above the title — where the two mobile panels put the drag handle instead, because a pointer has no drag gesture. It is the same band Sheet.Header shipped as on 2026-08-25 and to the same values, which is unsurprising: both were drawn on this artboard. Drawer has Title, Body and Footer and no Header part, so a caller composing that desktop panel built the row by hand. BUILT the same day as Drawer.Header — see 2026-08-25-drawer-header-ships-and-two-stale. Found while establishing that "Drawer Desktop" is a Drawer rather than a Sheet — all three panels here carry radius-lg on all four corners, a 1px border, shadow-md and a 4px inset, which is this component exactly and which a Sheet never is, being flush to three viewport edges with two corners and no border. That geometric test now sits beside the gesture test in CONVENTIONS §7a, for settling a static drawing where no gesture is visible to read. No code change.

The Drawer component sheet is updated in Paper, and one code correction falls out of it. Its layers now carry this component's own names: the band was called "Nav Group" and the body and footer were both "Primary Level Item", which is Sidebar's vocabulary on a Drawer — a sheet that cannot name its own parts cannot hand them off, and that is how Drawer.Header stayed unbuilt while being drawn. The desktop window frame is now named a DEVICE BEZEL: it is filled --ui-bg-emphasis-active where both mobile frames are filled --ui-scrim, so it shows the panel in isolation and says nothing about which edge the panel is anchored to, and reading it as a viewport is half of how this panel got mistaken for a Sheet. The band's three glyphs were HAND-DRAWN — a 16 viewBox, paths that exist in no icon set, on layers spelled "Checron Left" and "Checron Right" — and are now the real griddy exports with their layers named for the import. Which chevron was MEASURED rather than guessed: the drawn glyph is 5x9 in a 16 box (0.31 x 0.56), which matches ChevronLeftSmall (0.29 x 0.565) and not ChevronLeft (0.34 x 0.67), so drawer.stories.tsx is corrected from ArrowLeft/ArrowRight to the small chevrons. Their ink moves from --ui-text-secondary to --ui-text-primary, which is what chromeControl actually paints. The sheet also gains a Parts section and a Gaps section it never had, carrying the six rows this work produced — including the one that still needs a person, whether the desktop form drops the drag handle. Exported to design/paper/exports/component-drawer.pdf.

Drawer.Header ships, and two stale gaps close. The 48px chrome band is the row this component's own sheet draws on "Drawer Desktop" — back and forward chrome controls at the leading edge, a close at the trailing one — and it had never been built; Drawer had Title, Body and Footer and no Header, so a caller composing that panel built the row by hand. p-sm uniform, so 8 + 32 + 8 = 48 makes the padding and the pinned height agree rather than one of them being a second author of the inset. Sheet.Header's values exactly, both having been drawn on this artboard. It carries no scrolled hairline, unlike Sheet.Header: this sheet draws no scrolled state and inventing one is how a drawing stops being a contract. It is an ADDITION to the drag handle rather than a replacement — the handle is the drag affordance and the single-pointer alternative SC 2.5.7 requires, so whether the desktop form drops it is a question for design and is now in needsDesign rather than answered here. Separately: the story's two SELECT fields are real Selects now. They stood in as Inputs while Select did not exist, and the stand-in outlived its reason — the knownGap and a duplicate needsDesign row both said "there is no Select component in this system yet" while Select shipped.

check:motion joins the gate list, and every animating component now documents its motion. The gate rejects a literal duration or easing in registry/ (a discipline that was already perfect — zero hard-coded durations across 26 files — and had nothing keeping it that way), transition-all (CONVENTIONS section 6 has said this since the beginning and nothing enforced it), a keyframe with no reduced-motion guard, and an animating component with no top-level motion: note in its doc. It reads lib recipes alongside components as check:overlays does, so Header's motion is found in @/lib/chrome-control where it actually lives rather than reported as absent. 27 doc files gain a motion: note describing what moves, what drives it and what reduced motion does to it; Sheet's and ImageUpload's existing notes are PROMOTED out of a11y to the top level, where Button already had its, because motion is a description of what a component does rather than solely an accessibility concern and a field meaning one thing at two depths stops being findable. ImageUpload's note is corrected while being promoted: it credited the token layer with stopping its spinner, and what actually stops it is the motion-safe: variant. Two findings are recorded in the notes rather than fixed: Sidebar's collapsible section snaps via the hidden attribute where Accordion animates the identical interaction against Base UI's published height, and Banner reaches for transition-colors where the rest of the library enumerates properties. No component's rendered motion changes; no .tsx is touched.

migration.manual: Documentation only — every change is inside a *.doc.ts, and no component's classes or rendered motion moved. If you consume the doc files and read `a11y.motion`, it has moved to the top-level `motion` key on Sheet and ImageUpload; Button was already there and the other 27 are new.

changes.summary: Drawer takes snapPoints — resting heights as ascending fractions of the viewport — and the half-open state is now drawn in Paper (J88-0) rather than only described. Rendered in `dvh` rather than `vh`, because on mobile `vh` is the viewport with the browser chrome HIDDEN, so a 0.5 detent is not half of what anyone can see until the page has been scrolled. Opt-in throughout: omit snapPoints and the drawer keeps exactly its old behaviour, which the existing sixteen tests still prove unchanged. With detents a downward drag STEPS instead of dismissing and only dismisses from the shortest one — dragging a full-height drawer straight off the screen would skip the state the detent exists to offer, and is the surest way to lose whatever is in it. Upward drag is now honoured, having been deliberately clamped before, because rubber-banding up used to promise an expansion that could not happen. The accessibility work is the interesting half: the drag can now do THREE things, so SC 2.5.7 needs a single-pointer path for all three. The handle tap steps up and wraps from the tallest back to the shortest, covering expand and collapse; dismissal stays on the scrim and Escape. A tap that sometimes expanded and sometimes threw the drawer away would be worse than either. The handle also stops calling itself 'Close' once it resizes — that label is the only thing a screen-reader user has to go on. An empty snapPoints array falls back to the content-sized drawer rather than rendering a zero-height panel, because a caller computing that list can hand back an empty one.

Drawer — the bottom panel dismissed by dragging it down, and a SECOND overlay alongside Sheet rather than a variant of it. The distinction is the gesture, not the geometry: a Sheet is anchored to a side edge and closes on scrim or Escape; a Drawer carries a handle, follows the finger, and closes past a distance or a velocity. Adding side="bottom" to a Sheet would ship a drawer that cannot be dragged, which is the worst of both, so CONVENTIONS gains a §7a overlay taxonomy table (Popover / Modal / Sheet / Drawer) keyed on how each is dismissed and where it comes from — written after this pair was briefly collapsed into one component by mistake. Base UI supplies the focus trap, scroll lock, Escape and focus restoration (ADR 0012); the drag is ours, with no drag library entering the dependency list. Open state is held by the component rather than left to Base UI, because the handle has to close a drawer nobody is controlling from outside. Two decisions worth their own line. The handle is a real BUTTON as well as a drag target: WCAG 2.5.7 requires a single-pointer alternative to any dragging movement, and the honest one is the same control responding to a tap — not a second control hidden elsewhere. And it spans the full 32px band the sheet draws rather than the 8px bar inside it, because the bar alone would be an 8px target against SC 2.5.8's 24px floor. The velocity threshold measures the LAST segment of the gesture rather than averaging the whole of it — averaging punishes the common shape (grab, pause to read, then decide) by reporting a slow flick, and rewards a fast grab followed by a long hold with a flick it never made; the bug surfaced as a leisurely 40px test drag dismissing the drawer, because synthetically-dispatched events land within a millisecond of each other and made every drag read as infinitely fast. Design defects corrected in Paper: the scrim was --ui-bg-emphasis-active, an opaque surface role with no alpha, where --ui-scrim is the role that exists for exactly this; the panel used --ui-nav-bg and --ui-nav-border on a surface holding a form rather than navigation; the primary action was a raw --ui-blue-80; and the handle's radius was a literal calc(infinity * 1px) beside a --ui-radius-full on its sibling.

items.name: empty-state
items.title: EmptyState
items.lead: Explains what is missing and gives the reader a useful next step.

docs.lead: Explains what is missing and gives the reader a useful next step.
docs.name: EmptyState
docs.summary: The absence of content, explained: a mark on a well, a sentence saying what is missing, a second saying why, and the control that fixes it. Drawn on the sheet inside a Table's body, but it knows nothing about tables — the same block serves a filtered list, an empty inbox or a search with no results.

anatomy.notes: The outermost node. Owns className, the ref, the centred column and the 16px inset. No min-height: the draft's 133px is off the spacing scale and was its auto-layout's, not a designed value — and it never even applied, since the drafted block lays out at 160px. The container decides how tall an empty region is.
Mark, title and description as one 8px-gapped group, so the 16px gap to the action reads as the break between 'what happened' and 'what to do'.
The 32px sunken well. aria-hidden, and it sizes the glyph to 16 — griddy writes width="24" as a presentation attribute, so an unsized slot ships 24 whatever the sheet draws (§7).

A

, not a heading. See a11y.role.
The recovery, in prose.

docs.composition:
EmptyState
├─ icon?         ReactElement — a griddy glyph, unwrapped
├─ title         string (required)
├─ description?  string
└─ action?       ReactElement — a real Button, rendered as passed

icon.notes: Slot: the mark. The component owns the well and the 16px sizing; the icon is never wrapped (§3). Decorative by contract — the well is aria-hidden, because anything the mark means that the sentence does not is a sentence that needs rewriting.

title.notes: What is not here, in the reader's terms. Required: a picture and no sentence is a shrug. A string rather than a slot — there is no i18n runtime here (§9) and the caller owns the words.

description.notes: Why it is not here, and what would change that. 'Clear the status filter to see all 24 records' beats 'No results': it names the cause and implies the fix.

action.notes: Slot: the recovery. A real Button from the call site, rendered exactly as handed over — so its variant, size and handler stay visible where they are written rather than being inferred from props here.

do: Say what is missing AND why. A title alone leaves the reader guessing whether they broke something.
Pass a real Button as `action` so its variant and handler stay at the call site.
Give the container the live region when this REPLACES content — Table does it on the cell it renders this into.
Reach for Banner instead when something went wrong; an empty state describes an absence, not an error.
dont: Do not use it for a loading state. An empty region and one that has not arrived yet are different claims, and a reader who sees this while data is in flight is told the search failed.
Do not put an icon in that carries meaning the title does not — the well is aria-hidden.
Do not wrap the action to space it; the 16px gap belongs to the container (§3).
Do not give it a fixed height to fill a region. Size the region.

a11y.role:
A plain
. The title is a

, not a heading: the right heading level depends entirely on where this lands, and a component that guesses one breaks the outline of every page that guesses differently.
a11y.name: None of its own. The title is read as the content it is.

keyboard.does: Reaches the action, if one was passed. Nothing else here is interactive.

a11y.targetSize: Nothing here is a target. The action is a Button, whose sizes all clear SC 2.5.8's 24px floor.
a11y.focus: No focus treatment of its own — the action owns its indicator, as every control here does.
a11y.liveRegion: None by default, deliberately. An empty state that REPLACES what the reader was looking at needs announcing and one rendered with the page does not, and only the container knows which happened. Table marks the cell it renders this into aria-live="polite" for exactly that reason.

contrastPairs.role: the title, on a table body or a panel — the surface the sheet draws it on
the description
the mark on its well. aria-hidden, but a mark nobody can see is a 32px grey square, so it is held to the graphical floor rather than waved through as decoration

contrastPairs.why: The well behind the mark. It separates the glyph from the body and identifies nothing on its own — the title does that — so it is deliberately quiet: 1.19:1 light, 1.41:1 dark (on the 2026-11-03 warm-ink ramp sunken is a fill above the surface, so the well reads more in dark than in light).

forwarding.ref: The outermost node. Not a form control, so the §5 default applies.
forwarding.className: Lands on the outermost node, so padding or a min-height can be set from outside.
forwarding.rest: Native div props go to the outermost node — including `role` and `aria-live`, if the container wants them here rather than on itself.

needsDesign: The page-level size is drawn (sheet § Size: title `title-sm`, description `body-sm`, prompt gap 12, block gap 24, inset 32, text max-width 384, and the 32px well and 16px glyph deliberately unchanged) and is not implemented. What the sheet does NOT settle is whether it should be a `size` prop at all: every other size axis in this library is a prop, so the sheet assumes one, but this is the first whose two sizes differ only in type and space and could equally be a `className` at the call site.
knownGaps: One size ships. The sheet draws two — see `needsDesign`.

The title renders as a

. In a page-level empty state it is very likely the region's heading, and there is no `headingLevel` prop — pass one in via `aria-labelledby` on your own container, or wrap. Drawing the page size makes this more pressing, not less.
No loading variant, and none is wanted. An empty state and a not-yet-arrived state are different claims and this only makes the first; Skeleton makes the second.
The action is a single slot. A primary/secondary pair goes in as one element containing both buttons, which means the caller owns the gap between them.

contrast.role: the title, on a table body or a panel — the surface the sheet draws it on
the description
the mark on its well. aria-hidden, but a mark nobody can see is a 32px grey square, so it is held to the graphical floor rather than waved through as decoration

changes.summary: Public library pages follow the manifest and typed documentation, with article-inspired copy and no changing library totals. Public leads and categories feed generated HTML references, Markdown twins, gallery and search entries, agent indexes and registry routes. The optional NetworkCanvas renderer now has its own typed reference. New freshness, source-boundary, route/link and browser checks keep the public reader in step. Interactive specimens are a featured subset; hosting and the remaining release gates stay open.

The handoff sheet was drawn AFTER the component and validates it. All four needsDesign entries close the code's way: the description is caption/leading-normal rather than button-sm/leading-flat, there is no min-height (the draft's 133px is off-scale and was inert — the drafted block lays out at 160), a page-level size exists and steps type and space but not the 32px well, and dark is now drawn. Three defects in the draft the code had already avoided are recorded on the sheet rather than fixed here: the action was a pill with an outline and primary ink where Button is soft, inset-ringed and muted; two of the draft's three cases were ImageUpload's dropzone; and that dropzone's drag well was filled --ui-blue-80, a palette step rather than a role. No component code changed — only the doc, its design URL, and two comments that referred to the draft as 'the sheet'.

The absence of content, explained: a 32px sunken well carrying an aria-hidden mark, a 13px title, a 12px description and a slot for the control that fixes it. Every part but the title is optional, and the action is rendered exactly as passed rather than built from props. Two corrections over the sheet: the description was typed with --ui-text-button-sm — a BUTTON role on a line of prose — at leading-flat, which collides the moment the sentence wraps, so it ships as text-caption at leading-normal; and the container's off-scale min-height of 133px, which reads as an auto-layout artefact, is dropped so the container decides how tall an empty region is. It announces nothing on its own: a live region is the container's decision, because only the container knows whether this replaced something.

migration.manual: New item — nothing to migrate. `npx shadcn add @bydiorama/empty-state`; it pulls in `cn` and expects react as a peer. Pass a real Button as `action`, and give it aria-live yourself if you swap it in for content the reader was already looking at.

items.name: fade
items.title: Fade
items.lead: Softens an edge to show that content continues beyond it.

docs.lead: Softens an edge to show that content continues beyond it.
docs.name: Fade
docs.summary: An edge fade — the gradient that dissolves overflowing content into the ground it sits on, signalling continuation: under a pinned header, above a composer bar, at the cut of a truncated preview. One aria-hidden span, absolutely pinned to one edge of the caller's clipping container, painting a PERCEPTUAL ramp in the container's own bg role: a Gaussian penumbra sampled at seventeen stops (no corner at either end for the eye to read as a stripe), with a dark-scheme table that leaves the same perceptual fraction of ink visible as light does. Bound to a scroll container it eases out over the last band-depth of scroll instead of switching off, and keeps off a classic scrollbar. No new colour tokens: the ramp is an existing bg role, its depth the spacing scale (24/48/96). Elsewhere this pattern is a "scroll scrim" (GitLab) or "ScrollShadow" (HeroUI); here --ui-scrim already names the modal veil, so the fade keeps its own name.

anatomy.notes: The only node — an aria-hidden span, absolutely pinned to one edge, spanning the cross axis (less a classic scrollbar, when bound to a scroller), pointer-events none. It paints the ramp and nothing else. The CONTAINER is the caller's: position relative, the clipping (overflow-clip or a max-height), the ground the ramp ends on, and the route to the full content all belong there. An action slot (Show more, a 32px chrome control) is caller-composed and sits past the solid end of the ramp, never mid-band.

side.notes: The edge the content disappears under; the solid end of the ramp sits against it. Bottom is the default because truncation reads downward. Physical sides on purpose, like Sheet's: the band tracks the container's box — the geometry a scrollbar has — not the writing direction (knownGaps records the RTL consequence).

size.notes: Ramp depth on the spacing scale: sm 24px (space-xl) for dense chrome, md 48px (space-3xl) as the default, lg 96px (1.5 × space-4xl, the top of the scale and half again) for display-scale content and document previews — a three-line dissolve of body-md. One step deeper than the linear ramp's 16/32/64 because the Gaussian spends its first quarter under 9% alpha: a 48px eased ramp covers about what a 32px linear one did, and dissolves where that one ghosted (knownGaps, Ramp research). A caller who needs a depth sized to a type role sets --ui-fade-band-depth.

ground.notes: The bg role the ramp ends on — the CONTAINER's own ground, so every stop is one role at a different alpha. A fade painted in the wrong ground reads as a smudge (sheet § Grounds). `affix` is the translucent pinned-bar ground: the ramp scales by its 90%, so a band hung under that bar starts at the bar's own alpha and the two meet without a seam (Header uses it). Media is deliberately absent: text-over-image is ImageOverlay's contract; unknown or mixed grounds want fadeMask, not a painted colour.

isVisible.notes: Whether the band shows at all — opacity over --ui-duration-fast, never a ramp resize, which reads as the content moving. The band keeps its box either way, so toggling never reflows. On its own it is the right control for a non-scroll state (a bar parked or not, a preview truncated or not). With scrollContainer it is a gate on top of the scroll-linked strength: off means off.

scrollContainer.notes: The scroller this band belongs to — pass the element (hold it in state from a ref callback). The band then binds itself: its strength follows how much content runs past its edge, easing (smoothstep) from full to nothing over the last band-depth of scroll, so arriving at the end reveals the final lines as they arrive rather than in a 120ms pop at the last pixel. A band that is not inside the scroller is inset by the scroller's classic scrollbar on the cross axis — right (left in RTL) for a vertical band, bottom for a horizontal one — so it never veils the track or its arrows; overlay scrollbars measure zero and change nothing. Renders hidden until the first measure, server-side too. Strength is written to the band's own style, never React state, so scrolling re-renders nothing. Replaces wiring useScrollEdges into isVisible for the common case; the hook stays for callers that need the booleans.

className.notes: Lands on the band and merges last. The shipped use is placement nudges — `top-full` to hang a top fade below a pinned header, `top-auto bottom-full` to hang a bottom fade above a sticky region — and stacking context fixes. Cross-axis insets are the component's while bound to a scroller.

style.notes: Shallow-merged over the band's own (ADR 0014). The sanctioned override is --ui-fade-band-depth, which both the paint and the scroll-linked strength follow. The scroll-linked strength (--ui-fade-band-strength) is contract and cannot be overridden.

do: Give the container position: relative, the clipping (overflow-clip or a max-height), and the ground the ramp names — the band paints and nothing else.
Pair every fade with a reachable route to the full content: Show more, an expand control, or the scroll itself. The fade signals; the paired control discloses.
Bind a scrolling region with scrollContainer rather than wiring a boolean — the eased exit and the scrollbar inset come with it.
Under a translucent pinned bar, paint in ground="affix" so the ramp starts at the bar's alpha.
Put the action slot past the solid end of the ramp (the anatomy card's chevron sits 12px off the edge), never mid-band.
dont: Do not put anything interactive inside the band — mid-ramp ground fails every contrast floor by design, and the layer must not steal clicks (it is pointer-events none so content under it stays clickable).
Do not paint a fade over media or mixed grounds — no overlay colour is right there. Text over an image is ImageOverlay's contract; a ground-agnostic fade is fadeMask.
Do not use it as the only affordance — a fade with no route to the content is a defect, not a style (sheet § Behaviour, Affordance).
Do not animate the ramp's depth to show or hide it — that reads as the content moving. Visibility is opacity.

Do not hand-roll a two-stop ramp beside it (`bg-linear-to-t from-elevated to-transparent`). Its linear corners are the stripe this component was rebuilt to remove, and it cannot carry the dark correction — ChatWidget's was one, and it covered the last message even at the end of the scroll.

a11y.role: none — an aria-hidden span. The attribute sits AFTER the prop spread, so it is contract rather than default: paint never names anything (same reasoning as DotPattern).
a11y.name: None, ever.
a11y.focus: Never focusable and never a pointer target (pointer-events: none). Content under the band stays in the accessibility tree unclamped, stays selectable, and stays clickable — the band veils paint, not semantics. The conformance story for the faded region is the un-faded route (Show more, expand, scroll), which is a caller obligation the do/don't records. In forced-colors mode the painted ramp computes to none (CSS Color Adjust: a non-url background-image is reverted), so the content simply shows — the safe failure.

contrastPairs.why: Text mid-ramp sits under its own ground at ~40-48% alpha — below every floor, by design. The band is declared decorative like DotPattern's grain: nothing may depend on reading through it, which is why no interactive target may live inside it and why the un-faded route is mandatory. The dark-scheme table exists precisely because the same alpha left light-on-dark text MORE legible mid-ramp (3.81:1 against 2.95:1 at 50%) — a longer, dirtier trail, not a conformance gain.

forwarding.ref: Goes to the span — the only node, not a form control, so the §5 default applies.
forwarding.className: Lands on the span and merges last: placement utilities (top-full, bottom-full) displace the side's default pin. Bound to a scroller, the cross-axis inset is written to the band's style and wins over a className inset.
forwarding.rest: Native span props go to the span (a caller's data-slot replaces "fade" — ChatWidget's band keeps chat-widget-fade). `children` is typed out — the band is paint. `aria-hidden` is set after the spread and cannot be overridden.

docs.motion: One transition: opacity over --ui-duration-fast with --ui-ease-out — when isVisible toggles, and when a bound scroller moves the strength. The scroll-linked strength rides the same transition, which reads as the veil settling a beat after a fling stops rather than tracking every frame. 1ms under prefers-reduced-motion, handled at the token layer. Never the ramp's size. The static cue accompanying the motion (CONVENTIONS §8) is the content edge itself: at the flush edge there is visibly nothing more to scroll.
needsDesign: Horizontal fades are drawn at sm-to-md over chip rows; the eased lg (96px) has no horizontal row on the sheet. A carousel or kanban edge at that depth is a sheet row before it is a call site.

The sheet's action-slot chevron control (32px, bg-elevated, radius-md, ChevronDownSmall) is the same chrome control Header, Sheet and Calendar draw; Fade composes it from @/lib/chrome-control at call sites and does not own it. If a dedicated "expand" affordance becomes a pattern, it wants its own sheet row.
knownGaps: Ramp research (2026-11-02), the record of why the ramp is what it is. The two-stop linear ramp was rendered against the shipped copy beside smoothstep, smootherstep, sine, Larsen's scrim and a Gaussian at 32-96px, light and dark, over a document preview, a list, a chat column and a pinned header. Findings: (1) a linear ramp's corners read as a stripe with a start line, and at 32px over body-md it covered 1.5 lines — one line uniformly ghosted rather than a dissolve; (2) the scrim curve leaves the last line legible right at the edge, a hard cut of its own; (3) the Gaussian penumbra (mean 0.55, sigma 0.22) is the smoothest, and depth matters more than curve: three lines dissolve at ~96px, two at ~64; (4) at equal alpha light ink on a dark ground keeps more perceptual lightness (53% vs 46% at 0.5), so dark needed its own table — measured across five role pairs, the correction is the polarity's (±0.015). @/lib/fade-ramp carries the tables; its test re-derives them. Re-solved 2026-11-03 for the warm-ink dark ramp: 54% vs 46%, within ±0.02 across the pairs, no stop moving more than 0.006.

Progressive blur under a translucent bar — measured and DECLINED (2026-11-02). Continuing the bar's 8px backdrop blur down the band would remove the last difference between bar and band (blurred vs sharp at 10% visibility), but: an element with backdrop-filter is a backdrop root, so blur layers inside Header see nothing until Header's own blur moves to a child layer (verified in Chromium); any ancestor with opacity < 1, a filter or a mask silently disables it, including Fade's own opacity transition; and WebKit cannot be verified here — Playwright's WebKit drops backdrop-filter from screenshots headless and headed. The seam that WAS visible was the alpha step, and ground="affix" closes it. Revisit if a consumer's bar uses a heavier blur than 8px.

fadeMask is not reverted in forced-colors mode — mask-image is not a forced property — so a masked scroller keeps its faded edge for users who forced colours for contrast. It is an inline style helper, so it cannot carry a media query; the painted Fade has no such gap (its background-image is reverted). Use the painted band wherever the ground is a role.

Overlay scrollbars (macOS default) measure zero width, so a bound band still passes over an overlay thumb while it is shown. There is no API that reports an overlay bar's geometry; the classic-bar inset is what can be done. The contract test stubs the client box because headless Chromium hides scrollbars outright.

Mask mode, as `fadeMask`, is a style helper rather than a prop. A mask applies to the element being masked, so it lands on the CALLER'S scrolling container. It exists for grounds the painted ramp cannot serve: a brand-scoped surface whose fill is a project token, a document-defined canvas. The trade is real, which is why the painted band stays the default: a mask cuts every child that overlaps the band — the container's own scrollbar included — forces a compositing layer, and cannot be transitioned as cheaply as opacity. Measured trap: the prefixed and standard mask-composite are one property with two keyword sets, so writing the standard one first lets the legacy spelling win in Chromium.

Physical sides, so a left fade does not become a right fade in RTL. The band tracks the container's box like Sheet's side prop does; a consumer mirroring a layout in RTL flips the side themselves. start/end aliases are a conscious non-goal until an RTL consumer exists. (The scrollbar inset IS direction-aware: it reads the scroller's client box, which puts an RTL scrollbar on the left.)

No geometry spec (design/paper/specs/) exists for this item, deliberately — same decision as DotPattern: the geometry laws measure container/child insets, and an edge-pinned band is the shape they cannot express. The sheet's numbers — depth 24/48/96, full cross-axis span, flush to the pinned edge — are asserted directly in fade.browser.test.tsx instead.
The band needs a positioned ancestor, like every absolute layer: inside a static container it resolves against some ancestor and paints somewhere else. The type cannot stop a static container.

changes.summary: Public library pages follow the manifest and typed documentation, with article-inspired copy and no changing library totals. Public leads and categories feed generated HTML references, Markdown twins, gallery and search entries, agent indexes and registry routes. The optional NetworkCanvas renderer now has its own typed reference. New freshness, source-boundary, route/link and browser checks keep the public reader in step. Interactive specimens are a featured subset; hosting and the remaining release gates stay open.

Chat Progress rebuilt on StatusMatrix with ONE moving mark per turn. The CSS ring spinner is gone. New forms: waiting and streaming status rows (the thinking row's matrix hands over in place to its ending — failed and stopped keep the same element); reasoning under a five-line capped, faded body; a thought chain on a 16px node lane with kind glyphs, chips, prose, one level of branches, a failed status with Retry and a 40px tabular clock; parallel lanes drawn as the activity pill's box (glyph, 104px name, activity, clock, chevron) that open to their own chain. Only the deepest running node moves — the root when parallel or folded, none when isHeld — and a run that finishes while mounted folds to its receipt. Stop past ~30 s and a stoppedText ending. The geometry spec now measures the lane pill (sheet 4040-0) instead of the old step list.

migration.manual: BREAKING: steps take `status: "done" | "current" | "pending" | "failed"` with optional icon, duration, chips, detail and one level of `steps`; the spinner and its data-slot are gone (the row's mark is a StatusMatrix with data-slot="status-matrix"). Pass isHeld to every ChatProgress in a turn except the live edge. Rows are 17.55px at the body-sm role's leading rather than the old 16px.

changes.summary: Fade's two-stop linear ramp is replaced by a perceptual one (new lib item fade-ramp): a Gaussian penumbra sampled at seventeen stops, so there is no corner at either end to read as a stripe or a start line, plus a dark-scheme table that leaves the same perceptual fraction of ink visible as light does (light ink under a dark veil kept 53% of its lightness at 0.5 alpha against 46% in light, so dark trails lingered). Depths move one step to 24/48/96 (sm/md/lg) because the eased ramp's first quarter is under 9% alpha — md 48 covers about what linear 32 did, and dissolves where that one ghosted a single line. fadeMask uses the same profile as the paint's complement. Chosen by rendering six curves at four depths over the shipped copy in both schemes (fade.doc.ts, knownGaps 'Ramp research').

migration.manual: Callers that sized a layout around the band's depth (an action slot placed relative to a 32px ramp, a sticky region offset by -32px) re-check against 48px for md, 24px for sm and 96px for lg. To keep an old depth, set --ui-fade-band-depth on the band's style.

changes.summary: Fade gains scrollContainer and ground="affix". Bound to a scroller, the band's strength follows how much content runs past its edge, easing out over the last band-depth of scroll instead of popping off at the last pixel; it insets itself off a classic scrollbar (right, left in RTL, or bottom) instead of veiling the track; and it renders hidden until measured, server-side too. The strength is written to the band's own style, so scrolling re-renders nothing. ground="affix" paints in the translucent pinned-bar role, so the ramp starts at the bar's own alpha. useScrollEdges exports the measurement under it as scrollDistances(). Card.Body, Combobox and ChatWidget now bind their fades this way.

Fade ships — the edge fade / overflow gradient (a 'scroll scrim' elsewhere; here --ui-scrim already names the modal veil, so the fade keeps its own name), built the same day its sheet was drawn (Component --- Fade, artboard 2WCF-0). One aria-hidden span pinned to one edge of the caller's clipping container: side (top/bottom/left/right, physical like Sheet's — the band tracks the box, not the writing direction), size (sm/md/lg = 16/32/64 on the spacing scale, md deliberately matching ImageOverlay's shipped ramp), ground (base/surface/elevated/sunken restating the container's role so both gradient stops move together), and caller-owned isVisible toggling opacity on --ui-duration-fast. Zero new tokens. Findings the build sent back into the sheet: (1) the Ramp rule's 'transparent keyword greys the mid-band' claim was wrong — Tailwind's /0 modifier itself computes to transparent black through color-mix, and it cannot matter because gradient interpolation is premultiplied, so the browser test pins the transparent stop's ALPHA and the solid stop's ROLE, not the hue; the sheet's Behaviour and Grounds rows were corrected. (2) check:utilities refuses bare spacing steps on widths (the Modal max-w-md trap), so horizontal depths spell the token in parens (w-(--ui-space-2xl)) — same token, explicit name. (3) A wrong-element ref cannot be made to fail against a span host — HTMLSpanElement is structurally bare HTMLElement, so the covariant ref check accepts every element ref; the types test records the finding and the browser test asserts the runtime half. No geometry spec, deliberately (DotPattern's precedent): the laws cannot express an edge-pinned band, so fade.browser.test.tsx pins the sheet's numbers — depths 16/32/64 that all DIFFER, full cross-axis span, flush edge, four distinct ramp directions and four distinct grounds. Scroll binding stays caller-owned by design; the States story demonstrates the wiring with the scrollable region carrying role+name+tabIndex (axe's scrollable-region-focusable found the story shipping without them — the scroll is the fade's own disclosure route, so SC 2.1.1 applies to the composition).

items.name: header
items.title: Header
items.lead: Keeps the current context and the next action within reach.

docs.lead: Keeps the current context and the next action within reach.
docs.name: Header
docs.summary: The page's top bar: leading controls, an optional row of navigation items, trailing controls. A <header> so it is the banner landmark, but deliberately NOT a nav — the bar also holds a brand mark that links home and an avatar that opens the account menu, and calling all of that navigation would make the landmark useless to skip to. The item row names itself.

anatomy.notes: A <header>. 48px tall — PINNED (h-12), not emergent from py-sm around the tallest child: a bar whose tallest child is a 24px Header.Item used to render at 40px, silently. px-lg, bg-base — the PAGE ground, so the bar and the page it frames are one surface. Sidebar already painted bg-base; the bar was the outlier and in dark it sat below the page. Carries a transparent 1px bottom border at rest — see `affix` for why the hairline exists before it is visible. THE PAGE UNDER A HEADER MUST BE --ui-bg-base: the bar paints the page ground so the two read as one surface, and the affix Fade ramps to `base` for the same reason. That is an invariant on the CONSUMER, stated here because two shells in one app disagreed with it and nothing said so — one painted bg-surface, one a raw off-white. In light the mismatch is invisible (base and surface are 0.4% apart); in dark they are 20% apart and the ramp becomes a visible smudge under the bar. It is deliberately not a prop: the fade's ground is only correct if the bar's own fill moves with it, so a `ground` escape hatch on the ramp alone would let a consumer build a bar whose fill and ramp disagree — worse than the hardcoding it would relax.

The one state the bar changes into, set by the component itself once `affix` is on and the page has moved under it. Ground steps to --ui-bg-affix, the page's own fill at AFFIX_BG_ALPHA; an 8px backdrop blur turns what shows through into texture rather than competing text; --ui-shadow-lg lifts it; the resting hairline takes --ui-border-subtle. Nothing about the bar's geometry or contents moves. `data-affixed` is a public hook — style against it rather than re-deriving the scroll position.

Present only with affix={{ fade: true }}: a Fade (side=top, md, ground=affix) hung at top-full below the bar, visible only while data-affixed. ground=affix, not base (corrected 2026-11-02): the bar is the page at 90%, and a ramp starting at the page's solid 100% left a bright seam under the bar's edge; in the bar's own role the ramp starts at the bar's alpha. In this variant the ramp IS the separation — the shadow and the hairline colour stay off — and the page dissolves under the bar instead of sliding beneath an edge. aria-hidden, pointer-events none: it adds nothing to the banner landmark and content under it stays clickable. Drawn on the Header sheet (05 Affix · Affix + fade, both schemes) and on the Fade sheet's Pinned-header pattern.

Leading controls — the brand mark, which LINKS to the app home, and a back button, which is a button because popping history is an action. Slots: the caller supplies real elements with their own names.
A named <nav> wrapping a <ul> of items. gap-xs, p-xs.
A compact 24px control at 12px bold: px-sm, py-xs, radius-sm, with 16px icon slots. An <a> when given href, a <button> otherwise.
flex-1, aria-hidden. The sheet draws one on each side of the nav, which is what centres it.

A 32px chrome control with the menu glyph and a required label. It opens a Menu on desktop and a Sheet below the breakpoint — same button, two surfaces, chosen by the layout. NOTE: composed through either Trigger's `render`, the trigger's data-slot replaces this one — target it as `menu-trigger` or `sheet-trigger` there.
Trailing controls — a menu toggle, an Avatar.

docs.composition:
Header
├─ Header.Start          <a href="/" aria-label="… home">  <button aria-label="Back">
├─ Header.Spacer
├─ Header.Nav            label (required)
│  └─ Header.Item        href? isCurrent? icon? trailing?
├─ Header.Spacer
└─ Header.End            <Menu.Trigger render={<Header.MenuButton label="…" />} />  <Avatar …/>

Header.MenuButton opens ONE of two surfaces, and which one is a layout
decision rather than a prop:

  desktop  <Menu.Trigger  render={<Header.MenuButton …/>} />   the sections
  mobile   <Sheet.Trigger render={<Header.MenuButton …/>} />   the whole rail

Below the breakpoint the Sidebar is REMOVED rather than narrowed and the Sheet
carries it. NavRail is the OTHER answer to that question — a sibling component
at 48px, not a mode of Sidebar — and a layout picks one (ADR 0015).

affix.notes: Pins the bar (sticky top-0, z on --ui-z-sticky — the chrome layer, under every floating surface) AND lets it change into its affix state once the page has moved under it. ONE prop, not two: a bar that changes appearance without being pinned describes something that did not happen. Not a controlled `isAffixed` either — that would put a scroll listener in every consumer, which is the duplication this library exists to avoid. The state is OBSERVED, never listened for: an IntersectionObserver at threshold 1 with a -1px top root margin, which answers "am I stuck?" off the main thread and only when the answer changes. A scroll listener would fire every frame and need a getBoundingClientRect — a forced synchronous layout — to answer the same question. No sentinel element is involved. Turning `affix` off resets the state, so a bar toggled out while stuck does not keep a floating ground with nothing to float over. `{ fade: true }` is the VARIANT (CONVENTIONS §3's boolean-or-config shape): while affixed, a Fade — side=top, md depth, ground=base — hangs at top-full below the bar and the hairline and shadow-lg stay OFF, because the ramp is the separation. The ramp's ground is FIXED at `base` and takes no override, because what scrolls under the bar is the page and the page under a Header is --ui-bg-base (see the root part). Moving it alone would decouple the ramp from the bar's own fill (Header sheet 05 Affix · Fade variant; Fade sheet, Pinned header). The bar keeps bg-affix and the backdrop blur in both modes; `{}` behaves as `true`.

Nav.label.notes: Required — a page carries several navigations and <nav> landmarks are indistinguishable without names. Sidebar's rule, for the same reason.

Item.href.notes: OPTIONAL. With it the item is a real <a>; without it, a <button>. The sheet draws two items carrying a chevron that open menus rather than navigate, and a link that does not navigate is the commonest lie in a bar.

Item.target / Item.rel / Item.download /.notes: Item's props extend AnchorHTMLAttributes, so an external destination opens in a new tab through this API. They used to extend HTMLAttributes, which has none of these — the only way out was the `render` slot, which means writing the href twice and keeping the two copies in step. `type` is the one anchor attribute removed: on the button branch it is what stops a nav item submitting a form around it.

Item.isCurrent.notes: Sets aria-current="page" and makes the item RECEDE: no fill, ink stepped back to muted. You cannot navigate to the page you are on, so the items worth pointing at are the ones at full strength — an emphasised fill there spends the loudest thing in the bar on the least actionable item. FILL and INK are separate channels: fill answers the pointer (hover, on the current item too), ink says where you are. This replaced a four-step fill ramp that was wrong twice — first with hover and current sharing bg-hover, so the page you were on looked like the one under the pointer; then as four steps that ordered correctly in light and INVERTED in dark, 1.031 apart and backwards, because bg-elevated is a surface role and the surface scale inverts. With one fill left there is no ramp to order, which is the point. NOTE the divergence: Sidebar and NavRail still EMPHASISE their current row (nav-active-bg). A rail is a persistent map where the current row anchors you; a bar is a short row you read across. Confirm whether that difference is intended.

Item.trailing.notes: Slot: the sheet puts a chevron here on its two menu items.

MenuButton.label.notes: Required — it is the accessible name, and "Menu" is not one. Say what it opens. Pass the button to Sheet.Trigger's `render` so aria-expanded and aria-controls come from the Sheet: a button declaring its own disclosure state can disagree with the panel it opens, and nothing would catch it.

Item.render.notes: Slot: swap the item's own <a>/<button> for this element — pass render={<Link href={href} />} so the app's router owns the transition. Passed through, never wrapped (§3): the item's data-slot, aria-current and className merge onto it rather than replacing what it carries.

do: Match the Sheet to the button: Header.MenuButton in Header.End opens a Sheet with side="right", in Header.Start one with side="left". Sheet defaults to left, so the trailing case has to be stated — and a drawer arriving from the far edge reads as a different control entirely.
Name the nav; the landmark is otherwise anonymous.
Give an item an href only when it navigates — otherwise it is a button, and the chevron says so.

Make the brand mark a LINK to the app home, named for the destination — "Diorama home", never "Logo". The brand SWITCHER is a different control and lives in the account menu, and in the rail's profile layer on mobile.

Give Header.MenuButton a panel. A trigger with nothing behind it is the commonest way this pattern ships broken, which is why the desktop bar story composes the Menu rather than rendering the button alone.
Hide the nav row below your breakpoint; the sheet's mobile bar draws Start, a spacer and a menu toggle only.

Give `affix` a page that actually scrolls, and put the bar at the top of that scroll flow. Pinned to a page shorter than the viewport it is a prop that does nothing, which reads as broken rather than as unused.
dont: Do not wrap the whole bar in a nav. The banner holds more than navigation, and a landmark that contains everything helps nobody.
Do not convey the current page by ink alone — aria-current is what is announced, and it is the channel a screen reader has.

Do not render two Headers as siblings on one page. <header> is the BANNER landmark, a document may have exactly one, and axe fails on the second (landmark-no-duplicate-banner). A Header used as chrome inside a section is fine — the role only applies outside article/aside/main/nav/section.
Do not treat NavRail as Sidebar collapsed. They are sibling components (ADR 0015) and a layout renders one or the other; below the breakpoint this bar's menu button carries the navigation instead.
Do not put the mobile menu's panel here; that is a Sheet, and this bar only holds its trigger.

Do not hand-roll the affix state with your own scroll listener and a className. The ground is a token whose alpha is a measured conformance floor, the ink of the current item changes with it, and a bar assembled from `sticky` plus a shadow gets the first right and the second wrong — silently, and only in dark.
Do not add `sticky` yourself alongside `affix`; the prop already applies it, and a second `top` in `className` wins by merge order rather than by intent.

a11y.role: banner (from <header>), containing a named navigation landmark. Items in Start and End are not list items, because a brand switcher announced as one misdescribes the page.
a11y.name: The nav from its `label`. Every control in Start and End carries its own.

keyboard.does: Walks Start, then the items, then End — document order, the platform's own behaviour.
Follows a link item, or activates a button item. Native in both cases.

a11y.target: An item is a compact 24px control — SC 2.5.8's floor exactly rather than comfortably over it. See knownGaps.

contrastPairs.role: item labels on the bar — the bar is the page ground, so this pair is the page's own body contrast

the CURRENT item's label — it recedes rather than being emphasised, and a receding label is still body text: WCAG exempts disabled controls, not quiet ones. The bar's move to bg-base cost it the most on the old mid-grey dark ramp (6.47:1 on the bg-surface bar, 4.94:1 on bg-base); on the 2026-11-03 warm-ink ramp it is 5.93:1 light / 7.02:1 dark
the menu button's glyph on its chrome fill, and a nav item's label on the hover fill
the current item's label while it is hovered — the fill answers the pointer, the muted ink persists underneath it
the menu button's glyph while hovered

item labels while the bar is AFFIXED — measured against what can scroll under it (the fill at AFFIX_BG_ALPHA over black in light, white in dark) rather than against the page it floats over, which reconstructs the best case and would clear a bar that fails. 13.76:1 light, 13.16:1 dark

the CURRENT item's label while the bar is affixed — muted, exactly as on the resting bar: 4.75:1 light / 5.38:1 dark, the least headroom on the bar. It stepped up to secondary while the old mid-grey dark ramp put muted at 3.66:1 here (closed 2026-11-03)

contrastPairs.why: WCAG 1.4.3 exempts disabled controls, and a disabled chrome control has to read as unavailable — holding it to 4.5:1 would make it indistinguishable from an available one, which is the real failure. The chrome control has no doc of its own (it is a lib recipe), so its states are declared by the component that ships it.
contrastPairs.role: a disabled chrome control

needsDesign: The bar's inline padding is a raw 20px, off the spacing scale, and the design's own mobile bar uses 12. Shipped as 16.

`--ui-bg-selected` and `--ui-bg-hover` are the SAME value in theme zero's authored light map (neutral-90), which is why the item ramp cannot be built out of interaction roles alone. The contract's own note on bg-selected says "not hover"; the authored value makes it hover. Confirm whether a selected fill should sit past `bg-active` in light, as the derivation puts it.

The affix state is drawn LIGHT-ONLY on the Contacts page and in both schemes on the component sheet, but nothing draws the TRANSITION. The bar animates background-color, border-color and box-shadow at --ui-duration-base; whether the state should arrive that gently, or instantly, is a motion decision nobody has made.
knownGaps: CLOSED 2026-11-03 by the warm-ink dark ramp (ADR 0008 amendment): the current item stepped from muted to secondary while the bar was affixed, because muted measured 3.66:1 on `--ui-bg-affix-floor` in dark and no alpha closed it. It now measures 4.75:1 light / 5.38:1 dark, so the step is removed and the affixed bar keeps the sheet's muted current item. SiteHeader's quiet rest ink took the same step for the same reason and is removed with it.

Header.Item forwards a ref so it can BE a Menu trigger — the sheet draws 'Create' and 'Work' as nav items that open a menu rather than navigate. Compose them as `<Menu.Trigger render={<Header.Item trailing={<ChevronDown/>}>Create</Header.Item>} />`; note the trigger's data-slot then wins over `header-item`, which is true of every render slot here.
The sheet's bar uses a raw 20px inline padding, which is off the spacing scale entirely — and its own mobile drawing of the same bar uses 12. Shipped as px-lg (16); confirm with design.

The hover fill is `bg-elevated`, a SURFACE role — which is also what the chrome control resting beside it in the same bar is filled with, so a hovered nav item and a resting menu button are the same colour. It was a fill RAMP's second step when that mattered; now that the current item carries no fill, hover is the only one and moving it to `bg-hover` — the role named for the job — costs nothing. Left as the sheet draws it; one line to change.

Current is conveyed by ink alone, plus aria-current. `--ui-text-muted` on the bar measures 5.93:1 light / 7.02:1 dark (4.75 / 5.38 affixed), so it is legible, but a reader with reduced colour discrimination has only the weight-free ink difference to go on visually. The bar has no weight left to spend (12px bold already), which is what ruled out the Sidebar's approach. If that proves too quiet, the channels available are a rule under the item or an opacity step — both drawn decisions, neither taken.
No responsive behaviour of its own. The sheet draws a desktop bar and a mobile bar; which one shows is the caller's layout decision, not a prop.

The affix state is BUILT and its trigger is deliberately coarse: one boundary, one change. There is no scroll-linked ramp — no shadow that deepens with distance, no fill that fades in — because none is drawn and a continuous mapping from scroll position to appearance is a much larger promise than a state flip. If a ramp is ever wanted it needs its own drawing, not a tuning pass on this.

`affix` pins with `top-0`, fixed, and layers at `--ui-z-sticky` — the scale's chrome step, deliberately UNDER --ui-z-dropdown so a Menu opened from the bar itself (portalled to body) never slides beneath the translucent bar. A bar under another fixed element (a system banner, an editing toolbar) needs a different offset — not a prop yet; `className` is the escape hatch until a second caller needs one.

The observer roots itself at the nearest ancestor whose `overflow-y` scrolls, falling back to the viewport. Leaving it at the viewport default was a bug that HID: a bar pinned inside a scrolling panel sits at a fixed viewport position, so a viewport-rooted observer watches it never move and the state never flips — while the identical code works on a page that scrolls as a whole. It was caught by writing the test, not by looking at it. The walk-up reads `getComputedStyle` once per ancestor at mount; a container that becomes scrollable later is not re-detected.

A `position: fixed` bar is not supported — only `sticky`, which is what `affix` applies. Fixed removes the bar from flow, so nothing scrolls under it in the observer's terms and the state cannot be derived from geometry at all.
docs.motion: Nav items transition `background-color` and `color` at --ui-duration-fast with --ui-ease-out; the 32px menu toggle and avatar frame take theirs from `@/lib/chrome-control` rather than declaring their own, which is why this file carries only one transition for several moving parts. The BAR itself transitions `background-color`, `border-color` and `box-shadow` at --ui-duration-base (`motionStandard`, whose own comment names 'a bar's fill' as its case) — a surface arriving is not interaction feedback and should not move at interaction speed. `border-color` is animatable only because the hairline is present-but-transparent at rest; declaring the border in the affix state alone would make it a discrete swap AND jog the content lane by a pixel.

Header's affixed current item, and SiteHeader's affixed quiet items at rest, keep --ui-text-muted instead of stepping up to --ui-text-secondary. The step was a conformance workaround, not a design: on the old mid-grey dark ramp muted measured 3.66:1 on --ui-bg-affix-floor and no alpha closed it. Header's needsDesign entry on the step is closed. Visual: the affixed state of Header and SiteHeader, light and dark.

Header.Item gains variant="quiet" (the site bar's item, #33): label-md, 32px, no fill in any state, ink as the only channel — --ui-text-muted at rest, --ui-text-primary on hover and when current (the inverse of the default item, whose current page recedes; a row already at muted has nowhere to recede to). The default variant and the glyph form are unchanged.

Header's affix fade variant painted its ramp in the page's solid ground under a bar that is the page at 90%, so the strip just below the bar was MORE opaque than the bar — a bright seam exactly where the variant is meant to be seamless; it now paints in ground="affix" and starts at the bar's alpha.
