changes.summary: Header's affix prop widens to boolean | { fade?: boolean } (CONVENTIONS §3's boolean-or-config shape): affix={{ fade: true }} swaps the stuck state's edge-and-elevation treatment for a Fade — side=top, md depth, ground=base — hung at top-full below the bar and visible only while data-affixed. The ramp REPLACES the hairline colour and shadow-lg (the sheet's rule: the ramp is the separation); bg-affix and the backdrop blur stay in both modes, and {} behaves as true. Designed before building: the Header sheet's 05 Affix section gains 'Affix + fade' specimens in both schemes plus a Fade-variant annotation row, and the artboard moved to fit-content to hold them. First cross-item consumer of Fade, so @/ui/fade joined all four resolvers (root tsconfig, storybook tsconfig, vitest config, storybook main.ts) and header's registryDependencies. The browser suite compares the two affix treatments TO EACH OTHER while stuck (one bar carries the drop shadow, one the band — the Badge lesson) and asserts the band is Fade's own DOM (data-side/size/ground), not a re-implementation. Same session, on the Fade side: the BrandThemed story's fade read as missing because its copy could FIT the clip at wide panel widths — a fade over empty ground is invisible by definition — fixed with a fixed text measure (w-96) inside a 96px clip so the specimen truncates at every width; and the Fade sheet's Floating-bar pattern now clones the real Chat Composer from its own sheet (bg-field pill, radius-full, 1.5px border-subtle, 32px controls) in both schemes, replacing an invented bg-affix bar that complied with no component.

Header gains `affix` — one prop that pins the bar AND lets it change into its affix state once the page has moved under it. Not two props, because a bar that changes appearance without being pinned describes something that did not happen; not a controlled `isAffixed`, because that puts a scroll listener in every consumer. THE STATE IS OBSERVED, NEVER LISTENED FOR: an IntersectionObserver at threshold 1 with a -1px top root margin, which answers "am I stuck?" off the main thread and only when the answer changes, where a scroll listener fires every frame and needs a getBoundingClientRect — a forced synchronous layout — to answer the same question. No sentinel element. THE ROOT IS THE NEAREST SCROLLING ANCESTOR, not the viewport, and that was a bug that hid: a bar pinned inside a scrolling panel sits at a FIXED viewport position, so a viewport-rooted observer watches it never move and the state never flips, while the identical code works perfectly on a page that scrolls as a whole. It was caught by writing the test, not by reading the code. Painted: `--ui-bg-affix` ground, an 8px backdrop blur (`supports-` guarded — without the guard, a browser lacking backdrop-filter renders a translucent bar over sharp content, strictly worse than the opaque bar it replaced), `--ui-shadow-lg`, and the bottom hairline in `--ui-border-subtle`. THE HAIRLINE IS PRESENT AND TRANSPARENT AT REST so only its colour changes: declaring `border-b` in the affix state alone moves the content lane a pixel at the flip — border-box keeps h-12 at 48, so the padding box is what shrinks — and makes border-color a discrete swap instead of an animatable one. The bar transitions background-color, border-color and box-shadow at --ui-duration-base (`motionStandard`, whose own comment names "a bar's fill"), and that transition immediately caught its own test asserting rgba(255,255,255,0.95) — the halfway frame — as if it were the state. THE CURRENT ITEM STEPS FROM MUTED TO SECONDARY WHILE AFFIXED, and that is conformance rather than taste: muted measures 3.66:1 on --ui-bg-affix-floor in dark, under AA, and no alpha closes it. Secondary still reads as receding at 11.12:1 / 5.86:1. On the resting bar the current item is still muted, which is measured and unchanged. `data-affixed` is a public hook and the item reads it through a named group rather than a context, so a consumer restyling the current item has the same handle the component uses. Four browser tests measure the painted result after a real scroll in a real `overflow-y: auto` container — the case that caught the root bug.

check:motion joins the gate list, and every animating component now documents its motion. The gate rejects a literal duration or easing in registry/ (a discipline that was already perfect — zero hard-coded durations across 26 files — and had nothing keeping it that way), transition-all (CONVENTIONS section 6 has said this since the beginning and nothing enforced it), a keyframe with no reduced-motion guard, and an animating component with no top-level motion: note in its doc. It reads lib recipes alongside components as check:overlays does, so Header's motion is found in @/lib/chrome-control where it actually lives rather than reported as absent. 27 doc files gain a motion: note describing what moves, what drives it and what reduced motion does to it; Sheet's and ImageUpload's existing notes are PROMOTED out of a11y to the top level, where Button already had its, because motion is a description of what a component does rather than solely an accessibility concern and a field meaning one thing at two depths stops being findable. ImageUpload's note is corrected while being promoted: it credited the token layer with stopping its spinner, and what actually stops it is the motion-safe: variant. Two findings are recorded in the notes rather than fixed: Sidebar's collapsible section snaps via the hidden attribute where Accordion animates the identical interaction against Base UI's published height, and Banner reaches for transition-colors where the rest of the library enumerates properties. No component's rendered motion changes; no .tsx is touched.

migration.manual: Documentation only — every change is inside a *.doc.ts, and no component's classes or rendered motion moved. If you consume the doc files and read `a11y.motion`, it has moved to the top-level `motion` key on Sheet and ImageUpload; Button was already there and the other 27 are new.

changes.summary: The bar is --ui-bg-base, the PAGE ground, where it was --ui-bg-surface. It was the only piece of the shell answering a different role than the page it sits on — Sidebar already painted bg-base — and in light the difference was invisible (#FDFCFB against #FFFFFF, 0.4% apart), which is why it survived. In DARK the two are 20% apart and the surface scale inverts, so the bar sat BELOW the page ground it frames and the app chrome receded behind its own content. Nothing had drawn a bar and a page together until the index-page specimen did, which is the only reason it was ever visible. It fixes the hover ramp rather than costing one: --ui-bg-elevated against this bar is DARKER in both schemes (1.105 light, 1.168 dark) where against bg-surface it was darker in light and lighter in dark, so the hover fill now moves the same direction in both and the fill role is unchanged. Measured cost, and it is one pair: --ui-text-muted on the bar — the current item's receding label — goes from 6.47:1 to 4.94:1 in dark. Still over AA, and now the least headroom of any pair on this component; a step darker on --ui-bg-base in dark would spend it. Everything else gains: primary ink 12.55 to 9.59 dark and 16.76 to 17.17 light, both far over floor, and the chrome control's resting fill goes from 1.121 lighter to 1.168 darker in dark, matching its own light behaviour for the first time.

migration.manual: Nothing to change at a call site. If you pinned the bar's backgroundColor in a test or a visual baseline it is now --ui-bg-base (#FFFFFF light, #423E3A dark). If your app shell paints its page ground as something other than --ui-bg-base, the bar will no longer match it — that is the thing this change assumes, and the fix is the page, not the bar.

changes.summary: Two gaps a consumer hit while composing the bar across five app surfaces. (1) THE 48px HEIGHT WAS EMERGENT, NOT PINNED. The bar was py-sm around whatever its tallest child happened to be, which silently assumed a 32px control was present — so a bar whose tallest child is a 24px Header.Item rendered at 40px, and one route in an app had a shorter app bar than every other with nothing to say so. Both public call sites had already worked around it with their own h-12. The component now owns the height its own sheet specifies (h-12); py-sm stays, as the 32px content lane the sheet draws its controls in. The browser test mounts a bar containing nothing 32px tall and asserts 48. (2) Header.Item COULD NOT CARRY target/rel. Its props extended HTMLAttributes<HTMLElement>, which has no target, no rel, no download and no referrerPolicy, so an item pointing off the app could not open in a new tab through its own API — the only route was the `render` slot, which means writing the href twice and keeping the two copies in step. They now extend AnchorHTMLAttributes<HTMLElement>. `type` is the one anchor attribute removed: on the button branch it is the type="button" that stops a nav item submitting a form around it, and on an anchor it is a MIME hint nothing here wants.

migration.manual: A bar with no 32px control in it grows from its emergent height to 48px. If your app added its own `h-12` to compensate, remove it — the class merges either way, so leaving it is harmless. An external Header.Item routed through `render` purely to reach target/rel can drop the render element and pass target/rel directly.

changes.summary: The current page in a Header.Nav now RECEDES instead of being emphasised: no fill, ink stepped back to --ui-text-muted. You cannot navigate to the page you are on, so the items worth pointing at are the ones at full strength — an emphasised fill there spends the loudest thing in the bar on the least actionable item. FILL and INK become separate channels: fill answers the pointer, ink says where you are. Hover still applies to the current item ('hovering the current item did nothing at all' was the original defect and it stays fixed); the fill answers the pointer and the muted ink persists underneath it. This replaces the four-step fill ramp, and it dissolves that ramp's problem rather than tuning it: those four steps existed because hover and current shared bg-hover, then they inverted in dark because --ui-bg-elevated is a surface role and the surface scale inverts (hover 1.247 against the bar, current 1.210 — 1.031 apart and backwards). With one fill left there is no ramp to order, in either scheme. Measured: --ui-text-muted on the bar is 5.78:1 light / 6.47:1 dark, and 4.87:1 / 7.11:1 on the hover fill — both declared as contrast pairs, both clearing AA, because a receding label is still body text and WCAG exempts disabled controls rather than quiet ones. The browser test now asserts the two channels in both schemes rather than measuring a ramp. Two things recorded rather than decided: the hover fill is still `bg-elevated`, a surface role that is also the chrome control's resting fill, and moving it to `bg-hover` now costs one line; and Sidebar and NavRail still EMPHASISE their current row, which may or may not be intended — a rail is a persistent map, a bar is a short row you read across.

migration.manual: The current nav item loses its background and its label goes from primary to muted ink. Nothing to change at a call site — `isCurrent` is unchanged and still sets aria-current. If you styled around the current item's fill (an override, a screenshot baseline, a test pinning its backgroundColor), it is now transparent like every other resting item and the difference is in `color`.

changes.summary: Header.Item's fill ramp goes from three steps to four, and the third of them was a real defect: hover and current were BOTH --ui-bg-hover, so the page you were on looked identical to the one under the pointer, and hovering the current item changed nothing at all. It now runs transparent → bg-elevated (hover) → bg-hover (current) → bg-active (current AND hovered). Sidebar never hit this because its rows step from 500 to 600 as well as filling; a 12px bold bar item has no weight left to spend, which is why the bar needs a fourth fill where the rail does not. The steps are mutually exclusive by CONSTRUCTION — `not-data-[current]:hover:` — rather than by stylesheet order: `hover:bg-elevated` and `data-[current]:bg-hover` carry different modifiers, so tailwind-merge does not see them as conflicting, keeps both, and the winner would fall to the order Tailwind happens to sort variants in, which is exactly what cn() exists to prevent. The browser test asserts the four fills DIFFER rather than pinning four hexes, because pinning them would pass while any two silently converged; probed against the old code, where it reports three of the four as one value. Two further gaps closed alongside: the brand mark is now a LINK to the app home named for its destination rather than a button labelled 'Switch brand' (the switcher lives in the account menu and in the rail's profile layer), and the desktop bar composes Menu.Trigger around Header.MenuButton — the bare trigger with no panel behind it was the anti-pattern this component's own `dont` list names, sitting in the story every other story renders.

migration.manual: A nav item's hover fill is lighter than before and its current fill is unchanged. If you relied on hover and current looking the same, they no longer do — that was the bug. Callers rendering a bare Header.MenuButton should wrap it in a Menu.Trigger (desktop) or Sheet.Trigger (mobile); a trigger with no panel is unchanged in behaviour but was never intended.

changes.summary: --ui-bg-elevated is corrected in two ways, and both were only visible by measuring a running browser. (1) IN DARK IT OVERSHOT THE INTERACTION RAMP. Elevation raised 0.06 while --ui-bg-hover raises 0.05, so the raised SURFACE landed between hover and active: measured against --ui-bg-surface in theme zero's dark scheme, elevated 1.247 and hover 1.210. Every neutral ramp in the library is drawn as elevated → hover → active, so all of them inverted at their first rung, 1.031 apart — invisible AND backwards. Header.Item's four-step item ramp (the page you were on read quieter than the one under the pointer), the chrome control's rest → hover (hovering made it very slightly darker), and Multiselect's selected-vs-highlighted rows. Light was 1.079 / 1.188 / 1.434 throughout and never showed it, because theme zero AUTHORS light elevation and the derivation moves light elevation the opposite way from hover. Dark now raises 0.03 → 1.121, inside bg-hover in both schemes. (2) IT COULD COLLAPSE ONTO WHAT IT FLOATS OVER. A surface already at the top of the lightness range cannot be raised, so a brand seeded with surface #ffffff got elevated == surface. For a modal that is survivable — its border and shadow carry the separation — but the chrome control and a Header item's hover are a FILL WITH NO EDGE, so it meant no control and no hover feedback at all. When the raise measures as nothing the derivation now steps down instead. Two resolver tests enforce it across every stress brand and both schemes: the neutral fill stack must be ordered by MEASURED contrast (elevated < hover < active, with a real margin), and elevated must measure at least 1.02 against surface. Found by a consumer measuring computed styles in a real browser, not by reading code.

migration.manual: Dark-scheme cards, menu panels, chrome controls, dropzones and table mats are one step less raised than before (1.247 → 1.121 against bg-surface); their ink contrast improves accordingly. Nothing to change at a call site. If you pinned a dark bg-elevated hex in a test or a screenshot baseline, re-take it. A brand theme whose `surface` is pure white now gets a recessed bg-elevated rather than one identical to the surface — if you compensated for the collapse with a local override, remove it.

changes.summary: A Sheet opens from the edge its trigger sits on. Header's own story put the menu button in Header.End and let Sheet's `side` default to left, so the drawer flew in from the opposite edge to the control the user had just pressed — reported, and right: the two read as different controls. The composition is corrected to side="right", the rule is stated in both Header's and Sheet's do-lists, and a browser test asserts the RELATIONSHIP rather than coordinates — the button is past the viewport midpoint and the panel shares that edge. Not enforceable in a type, because the Sheet root wraps the Header and cannot see which region its trigger landed in.

Header.Item forwards a ref, which is the whole of the Header/Menu refactor. The sheet draws 'Create' and 'Work' as nav items that open a menu rather than navigate — the component already rendered a <button> with a `trailing` chevron slot for exactly that, and its own comment said so, but without a forwarded ref the behaviour layer could not anchor a panel to the row or restore focus to it, and the failure is silent. Composing is now `<Menu.Trigger render={<Header.Item trailing={<ChevronDown/>}>Create</Header.Item>} />`. The browser test asserts ONE element rather than a button inside a button, that focus returns to the row on Escape, and that the composed row keeps the same computed geometry as a plain item beside it. Sidebar was assessed and deliberately NOT changed: its collapsible sections are an inline disclosure, which is a different pattern from a menu, and whether the Menu panel should adopt it is the open design question recorded in menu.doc.ts.

Header navigation items now use the library's compact-control anatomy: an 8px inline and 4px block inset, a 4px soft radius, 4px between adjacent items, and 16px leading and trailing icon slots. This replaces the fully-pill 999px radius, 4px all-around inset, 12px inter-item gap, and unconstrained Griddy glyphs that rendered at their 24px default. The browser regression asserts the computed padding, radius, gap, target height, and rendered SVG box against the exported Paper header and the same radius-sm / px-sm / py-xs recipe used by other compact controls.

Header.MenuButton — the control the navigation collapses INTO, and the reason it is a named part rather than an anonymous child is that it carries the whole responsive story. There is no rail: below the breakpoint the Sidebar is not narrowed, it is REMOVED, and this button is what remains of it, opening the same Sidebar inside a Sheet. A rail is a different answer to the same question and can arrive later without changing any of this, which is why the pattern is not built as a step toward one. It renders the shared chrome control — the 32px bg-elevated square the sheet actually draws — where the stories had been using a ghost Button, transparent and ringless, which is a different thing the design does not draw in that bar; the visual matrix carried the same mistake and now shows both the leading control and the menu button on the same recipe. `label` is required because "Menu" is not an accessible name, and the button is meant to be passed to Sheet.Trigger's `render` so aria-expanded and aria-controls come from the Sheet: a button declaring its own disclosure state can disagree with the panel it opens and nothing would catch it. One trap found and recorded while wiring it: a part composed through `render` LOSES its own data-slot — Sheet.Trigger's wins, because there is only one element — so the composed button is targetable as `sheet-trigger` and not as `header-menu-button`. That is true of every render slot in this library, and a selector written against the part's own slot silently matches nothing, which reads as the component having failed to render. `check:controls` also learned that a <button> in a file importing chromeControl needs no exemption; it is the sanctioned path, and demanding an allowlist entry for correct code fills the allowlist with things nobody needs to read.

Header — the page's top bar, and a deliberate refusal to make the whole thing a nav. It renders a <header>, so it is the banner landmark, but the navigation landmark is the item ROW alone: the bar also carries a brand switcher, a back button, a menu toggle and an avatar, and a nav landmark containing all of that is one nobody can usefully skip to. For the same reason items inside the row are list items and controls in Start and End are not — a brand switcher announced as a list item misdescribes the page. An item is a real <a> when given an href and a <button> otherwise, because the design draws two items carrying a chevron that open menus rather than navigate, and a link that does not navigate is the commonest lie in a bar. Design defects recorded rather than transcribed: the bar's inline padding is a raw 20px, off the spacing scale entirely, and the design's OWN mobile drawing of the same bar uses 12 — shipped as px-lg with the discrepancy flagged; and no current state is drawn at all, so isCurrent exists because a nav needs one and its fill is derived from --ui-bg-hover. The 24px item pill is SC 2.5.8's floor exactly rather than comfortably over it, which is the design's number and is recorded as a gap rather than quietly enlarged.

items.name: image-edit
items.title: ImageEdit
items.lead: Adjusts an image before it is used.

docs.lead: Adjusts an image before it is used.
docs.name: ImageEdit
docs.summary: A crop stage with zoom and optional rotation. The crop WINDOW is fixed and the image moves behind it — by drag, and by the arrow keys, which the sheet draws no path for. Rectangular or circular; the circle is the avatar case, where the mask matches the destination. It is the body of a dialog, not the dialog: the caller wraps it in Modal and supplies the title, the close and the footer.

anatomy.notes: The column: stage, then one control per adjustment. Carries className, the ref, and data-shape.
The media ground and the pointer/keyboard target. Focusable, role=group, named by cropLabel and described by the keyboard hint. Painted --ui-bg-media, not --ui-bg-emphasis.
The picture. Drawn ONCE, across the whole stage, and it carries the alt text. Its fitted size is measured on load and on resize; every guarantee below is computed from it.

The window. Fixed size, edged in ink-on-media, and the source of the dimming: a box-shadow with a spread larger than the stage puts a hole in the scrim, so it follows the border-radius and the circular mask gets a circular hole. 240x168 rect, 168px circle.
The rule-of-thirds grid, shown while the stage is pressed. aria-hidden.
Corner marks, rect only. DECORATION — the window does not resize, so they carry no handlers.
A label row plus a Slider. One for zoom, one for rotation.

docs.composition:
Modal
└─ Modal.Surface
   ├─ Modal.Title            "Adjust image"
   ├─ ImageEdit
   │  ├─ src / alt           required
   │  ├─ shape?              "rect" | "circle"
   │  ├─ zoom? / defaultZoom? / onZoomChange? / minZoom? / maxZoom?
   │  ├─ hasRotation?        draws the second control
   │  └─ rotation? / defaultRotation? / onRotationChange? / maxRotation?
   └─ Modal.Footer
      ├─ Button variant="outline"   Cancel
      └─ Button                     Apply

alt.notes: The picture is the whole subject of the dialog. A cropper whose image announces as nothing leaves a screen-reader user adjusting an unnamed thing.

shape.notes: rect is 240x168 with corner marks; circle is a 168px mask for the avatar case. The circle deliberately has no corner marks — a round crop cannot deliver the rectangle a corner handle promises, and the sheet draws none on that row.

zoom.notes: A percentage of the COVER FIT, not of the picture's own size: 100% is the smallest scale at which the picture fills the crop at its current rotation, so the crop can never contain a hole. It was previously a percentage of 'contained in the stage', which promised nothing about the crop — a 600x3000 picture fitted to 52x260 against a 240px-wide crop left 188px of nothing in the middle of the result. Controlled or uncontrolled through defaultZoom, via the shared useControllableState (§4).

hasRotation.notes: Draws the rotation control. The sheet shows three rows without it and one with, so it is opt-in rather than always present.

rotation.notes: Degrees, clamped to ±maxRotation (45 by default). This is straightening, not orientation — a 90° turn is a different action and is not drawn. Rotating at 100% visibly GROWS the picture, and it has to: the crop's rotated bounding box grows faster than the picture does (240x168 needs 283x240 at -20°), so holding the scale would open the corners.

cropLabel.notes: Names the stage, which is the focusable region a keyboard user lands on.

keyboardHint.default: "Use the arrow keys to move the image inside the crop."
keyboardHint.notes: Rendered sr-only and referenced by the stage's aria-describedby, so the keyboard path is announced rather than discovered. The sheet draws no keyboard affordance at all.

do: Wrap it in a Modal and supply the title, close and footer — it is the dialog's body, not the dialog.
Read zoom and rotation from your own state on Apply; the pan offset is internal and deliberately not exposed.
Use shape="circle" whenever the destination is round, so the mask matches what the user will actually get.
Translate cropLabel and keyboardHint along with everything else — they are props for that reason.
dont: Do not expect the crop window to resize; the window is fixed and the image moves. That is what the sheet draws, and it is why the corner marks carry no handlers.
Do not read `zoom` as a fraction of the picture's natural size — it is a fraction of the cover fit, so 100% means 'exactly fills the crop' and never means 'actual size'.
Do not paint the stage with --ui-bg-emphasis. That role IS the accent, so a brand seed turns the stage into its brand colour and every colour in the picture is judged against it.
Do not remove the keyboard hint to save space — it is the only announcement of the one interaction the sheet never drew.
Do not use it for a 90° rotate or a flip; this control straightens, and neither is drawn.

a11y.role: The stage is role=group with a name and a description — a focusable region, not a widget with a value. The two adjustments are real Sliders, which carry their own roles and values.
a11y.name: cropLabel names the stage; the picture's alt names the image; each Slider is named by its own label, rendered sr-only because the visible row uses different type roles.

keyboard.does: Moves to the stage, then to each slider and its steppers.
Move the image inside the crop, 8px at a time. The path the sheet does not draw.
Move it 32px at a time.
Step the zoom or the rotation. Base UI's, not re-implemented.

a11y.pointer: Dragging the stage pans the image, with pointer capture so a drag that leaves the stage keeps tracking. preventDefault is called only for keys this control handles, so Tab and Escape still leave the dialog.

contrastPairs.role: the crop window's edge and its corner marks, against the palest ground the media family guarantees — the boundary that identifies the crop
a control's label
a control's value readout

contrastPairs.why: The same marks against the stage at FULL strength rather than against the family's guaranteed floor — measured 15.53:1 in both schemes. It is declared because it is what is actually painted when no picture has loaded, and it is decorative rather than a second non-text claim because the floor pair above is the stricter one and already carries the conformance argument.

forwarding.ref: Goes to the outermost node. ImageEdit is not a form control — its two values are the Sliders', which own their own elements.
forwarding.className: Lands on the outermost node.
forwarding.rest: Native div props go to the outermost node.

needsDesign: No keyboard path is drawn for the crop. Shipped with arrow keys panning the image (Shift for a coarse step) and an sr-only hint on the stage, following CardSorting's precedent. This is MINE, not the sheet's — confirm the keys and whether the hint should also be visible.

The stage is drawn --ui-bg-emphasis, which is the accent: under a pale-yellow brand seed it resolves to #ffe066 and a photograph is judged against bright yellow. Shipped on --ui-bg-media, the neutral media ground. Confirm.

Both sliders are drawn with a --ui-bg-accent fill (1.24:1 against their own track) and a --ui-border-default knob edge (1.76:1 against the track, 2.14:1 against the knob's own fill). Shipped as the Slider component, whose fill and thumb ring are floored at 3:1. This is the fourth sheet in a row to draw a value with the raw accent.
The panel's shadow is a raw #1D1B1929 rather than --ui-shadow-sm, which is the same value on the token layer. The panel is Modal's in code, so this is a note for the sheet.
Cancel is drawn outlined in --ui-border-default (2.14:1). Shipped as Button variant="outline", which uses --ui-border-control at 3.11:1 — the same finding already recorded against Button.

The corner marks read as resize handles but the window does not resize in any drawn state. Either they should go, or the crop should be resizable — which is a much larger interaction and would need its own keyboard contract.
No hover, focus, disabled or loading state is drawn for the stage. It takes the system focus ring.
The 'Dragging' row shows the thirds grid and says the surround lifts, but gives the dimming outside the crop no value. Shipped as the media ground at 64% over the picture. Confirm.

Zoom's baseline. The sheet labels the resting state 100% but does not say what it is 100% OF. Shipped as the COVER FIT against the crop at the current rotation, so 100% is a true floor and the crop is always full; the visible consequence is that rotating at 100% grows the picture. The alternative reading — 100% of the stage fit — leaves a hole in the crop for any portrait or panoramic picture, and opens the corners past about ±20° of rotation. Confirm.

The rotation track is drawn BIPOLAR — fill from the centre out, plus a 2x12 centre tick in --ui-border-strong marking 0°. Slider has one fill origin, so it is shipped filling from the minimum and without the tick; see knownGaps. If bipolar sliders are going to recur (a straighten, a balance, an offset), that is an `origin` prop on Slider rather than a local workaround here.
knownGaps: The cover fit is computed from the picture's fitted box, which is only known once it has loaded. Between mount and load the scale is 1 and the crop may briefly show the stage — one frame for a cached image, longer for a slow one. There is no loading state drawn to cover it.

The rotation slider fills from its MINIMUM, not from zero. The sheet draws a bipolar track — the fill runs from the centre out to the thumb — and Slider has one origin. The thumb sits in the right place and the value announces correctly, so this is cosmetic, but it makes −12° look like 'a third of the way along' rather than 'a little to the left of straight'. Fixing it properly means an `origin` prop on Slider, which is a second API change and is not worth making blind.

The sheet's centre tick on the rotation track — a 2x12 mark in --ui-border-strong at 0° — is not drawn, for the same reason. It is the thing that shows where 'straight' is, so it is the more useful half of the bipolar treatment.

The pan offset is not exposed. A caller gets zoom and rotation on Apply and must render the result itself; producing the cropped bitmap is the app's job, since it involves a canvas and this library has no data layer (§9).
Rotation is straightening only (±45° by default). A 90° turn or a flip is a different action and neither is drawn.
The thirds grid appears on pointer press only. A keyboard user panning with the arrows does not see it, because there is no drawn state that says they should.
The two copies of the picture mean the image is fetched once but decoded twice; at these sizes that is cheaper than a canvas and it is what the sheet's own layer tree does.
docs.motion: One transition: the rule-of-thirds guide fades in on `opacity` at --ui-duration-fast with --ui-ease-out while the stage is being dragged. The image itself is direct manipulation — it follows the pointer with nothing interpolating between positions, because a transition there would lag the drag.

contrast.role: the crop window's edge and its corner marks, against the palest ground the media family guarantees — the boundary that identifies the crop
a control's label
a control's value readout

changes.summary: Public library pages follow the manifest and typed documentation, with article-inspired copy and no changing library totals. Public leads and categories feed generated HTML references, Markdown twins, gallery and search entries, agent indexes and registry routes. The optional NetworkCanvas renderer now has its own typed reference. New freshness, source-boundary, route/link and browser checks keep the public reader in step. Interactive specimens are a featured subset; hosting and the remaining release gates stay open.

Slider's keyboard focus ring was declared and never painted. Base UI focuses the native input[type=range] INSIDE the thumb, never the thumb div, so `focus-visible:shadow-(--ui-focus-ring)` on the div matched nothing — every gate was green because the class resolved and the token existed, and no test had ever focused a slider and looked. The thumb now keys off `has-focus-visible:` (and so does the forced-colors outline), keeping --ui-shadow-sm beneath the ring as the sheet draws it. The same mistake hid the disabled ring: `disabled:` on a div never matches, so it now keys off Base UI's data-disabled. The group also carries aria-disabled when disabled, so its label and value read as parts of a disabled control rather than as low-contrast text. Probed: the browser test fails against the shipped class with no focus colour in the computed shadow. Paper: https://app.paper.design/file/01KZ39A2BC286MT85M658NRR4R/p-Z-0 (Component --- Slider --- Revision / Variants / Dark / API, Behaviour, Tokens, Gaps). Consumers with a copied slider.tsx should take the thumb class.

check:motion joins the gate list, and every animating component now documents its motion. The gate rejects a literal duration or easing in registry/ (a discipline that was already perfect — zero hard-coded durations across 26 files — and had nothing keeping it that way), transition-all (CONVENTIONS section 6 has said this since the beginning and nothing enforced it), a keyframe with no reduced-motion guard, and an animating component with no top-level motion: note in its doc. It reads lib recipes alongside components as check:overlays does, so Header's motion is found in @/lib/chrome-control where it actually lives rather than reported as absent. 27 doc files gain a motion: note describing what moves, what drives it and what reduced motion does to it; Sheet's and ImageUpload's existing notes are PROMOTED out of a11y to the top level, where Button already had its, because motion is a description of what a component does rather than solely an accessibility concern and a field meaning one thing at two depths stops being findable. ImageUpload's note is corrected while being promoted: it credited the token layer with stopping its spinner, and what actually stops it is the motion-safe: variant. Two findings are recorded in the notes rather than fixed: Sidebar's collapsible section snaps via the hidden attribute where Accordion animates the identical interaction against Base UI's published height, and Banner reaches for transition-colors where the rest of the library enumerates properties. No component's rendered motion changes; no .tsx is touched.

migration.manual: Documentation only — every change is inside a *.doc.ts, and no component's classes or rendered motion moved. If you consume the doc files and read `a11y.motion`, it has moved to the top-level `motion` key on Sheet and ImageUpload; Button was already there and the other 27 are new.

changes.summary: Slider's steppers take optional `decrementIcon` / `incrementIcon` slots, defaulting to the existing −/+. A stepper's MARK depends on what is being stepped, not only its label: Image Edit steps a rotation, where the two ends are counter-clockwise and clockwise rather than less and more, and the sheet draws curved arrows there. The labels already varied for exactly that reason; this is the visual half of the same fact. Additive — every existing Slider renders unchanged.

migration.manual: Additive. Pass `decrementIcon`/`incrementIcon` alongside `hasSteppers` to replace the −/+ glyphs; omit them and nothing changes.

changes.summary: Three defects found by looking at the built Storybook. (1) ImageEdit drew the picture TWICE — dimmed across the stage and again inside the crop — and the two could never align: each was object-contain inside a different box (384x260 against 240x168), so they resolved to different scales and offsets, and rotating showed both quads at once. Now one image, with the crop dimming everything outside it via a box-shadow whose spread exceeds the stage; that also follows border-radius, so the circular mask gets a circular hole for free. (2) Slider's thumb overhung the track at both extremes, because Base UI centres it on the value — at the minimum half of it sat outside the track and inside the 8px gap to the stepper button. The control is now inset by half a thumb, so the thumb's OUTER edge lands on the control's edge and the track it travels is the track it paints. Reported against Image Edit; it was every slider at 0 and at 100. (3) Thumbnail gains isLoading — a centred CSS spinner on the well, with the withheld, announced as role=status named after the file. Thumbnail.Group's stacked spread now eases out over --ui-duration-slow to a ZERO gap rather than snapping to +4px on the standard curve: half the travel, and all the interaction needs, since what the overlap hides is the next tile's top-right corner where the remove control sits.

migration.manual: Slider renders slightly differently at every size: the track is inset by half a thumb (8px each side; 12px at lg), so a track measures 16-24px narrower than before and the thumb no longer overhangs. No API change. Thumbnail's `isLoading` is additive and defaults to false.

changes.summary: Zoom is now a percentage of the COVER FIT against the crop, at the current rotation — not of the picture contained in the stage. The old baseline promised nothing about the crop, which is the only thing the user gets back: a 600x3000 picture fitted to 52x260 left 188px of nothing inside a 240px-wide crop, a panorama left 91px, and rotation opened the corners on pictures that were fine at 0° because the crop's rotated bounding box grows faster than the picture does (240x168 needs 283x240 at -20°, against a fitted 16:9 of 384x216). So a cropper could hand back a crop with a hole in it. The pan is clamped to the same geometry and re-clamped on read, since zooming out or straightening shrinks a limit that was legal a moment earlier. Both were blocked on one missing fact — the picture's fitted size — which is now measured on load and on resize, closing the unbounded-pan knownGap too. Visible consequence: rotating at 100% grows the picture, because it must. Found by the maintainer looking at Storybook; the coverage suite fails against the previous version in seven places.

migration.manual: `zoom` means something different: 100% is now 'exactly fills the crop' rather than 'fits the stage'. A caller passing a zoom read from the old behaviour will see a larger picture. minZoom=100 is now a meaningful floor rather than an arbitrary number.

changes.summary: A crop stage with zoom and optional rotation, in the sheet's two shapes. The crop WINDOW is fixed and the image moves behind it, which is what the sheet actually draws — the corner marks are decoration, and the circular avatar row has none because a round crop cannot deliver the rectangle a corner handle promises. It is the body of a dialog rather than the dialog: Modal supplies the surface, title, close and footer. Four fixes: the stage is --ui-bg-media rather than --ui-bg-emphasis, which IS the accent and resolves to #ffe066 under a pale-yellow brand seed; both adjustments are the Slider component rather than the sheet's hand-drawn track, whose fill measured 1.24:1 and whose knob edge measured 1.76:1 against the track; Cancel is Button variant=outline (3.11:1) rather than the drawn --ui-border-default (2.14:1); and the sheet draws NO keyboard path for the crop at all, so arrow keys pan the image with Shift for a coarse step, announced through an sr-only hint on the stage. That last one is an invention and is recorded as mine under needsDesign.

migration.manual: New item — nothing to migrate. `npx shadcn add @bydiorama/image-edit`; it pulls in `cn`, `slider` and `use-controllable-state`, and expects react and griddy-icons as peers.

items.name: image-overlay
items.title: ImageOverlay
items.lead: Keeps a label readable over an image.

docs.lead: Keeps a label readable over an image.
docs.name: ImageOverlay
docs.summary: A picture with content on top of it. `scrim` darkens the bottom and holds a caption; `full` covers the whole frame, blurs it and centres an action. The veil is strong enough that its inks clear AA over the brightest possible photograph — which is the only guarantee a component that puts text on unknown images can make.

anatomy.notes: The AspectRatio frame itself, not a wrapper around one — same ratio, radius, clip and well, so the two cannot drift. It carries className and the ref, and its data-slot is REPLACED with image-overlay, so `[data-slot="aspect-ratio"]` does not match inside one.
A real , sized and cropped by the frame. Carries the alt text.
The darkened region. Pinned to the bottom edge in `scrim`, covering the frame with an 8px backdrop blur in `full`.
scrim only. A 32px transparent-to-veil ramp ABOVE the caption. aria-hidden — it is the picture dissolving, not content.
scrim only. The caption's ground, at the veil's full strength so every line sits on the same measured surface.

The first line, at the sheet's 16px/600. Inset by --ui-space-xs per §6, clamped to one line. It uses `body-lg` at bold weight rather than `title-sm`: the title roles are FLUID, and a caption lives inside a frame whose width comes from a grid column rather than from the viewport, so title-sm computed to 12.17px against the sheet's 16.
The second line. Same inset, quieter ink, still AA.

docs.composition:
ImageOverlay
├─ src        string (required)
├─ alt        string (required) — "" for a decorative picture
├─ ratio?     AspectRatio's six named ratios
├─ variant?   "scrim" | "full"
└─ children   what sits on the veil

<ImageOverlay src="/cover.jpg" alt="Abstract gradient" ratio="square">
  <Badge variant="success">Approved</Badge>
  <ImageOverlay.Title>Abstract background</ImageOverlay.Title>
  <ImageOverlay.Description>Photo Library</ImageOverlay.Description>
</ImageOverlay>

<ImageOverlay src="/cover.jpg" alt="" variant="full">
  <Button variant="secondary">Download</Button>
</ImageOverlay>

src.notes: The picture. A real , so a broken URL degrades to the alt text rather than to an empty box.

alt.notes: Empty string for a decorative picture. Required rather than optional because an image carrying a caption is usually NOT decorative, and the caption is a different sentence from the alt text: the caption names the asset, the alt text says what it looks like.

ratio.notes: Passed straight through to AspectRatio. Same vocabulary, same meanings — there is no second ratio scale here.

variant.notes: scrim holds a caption at the bottom edge. full covers the frame, blurs the picture behind it and centres its children — the sheet fills it with a single action, which is what it is for.

children.notes: Anything. A Badge sits flush at the veil's padding because it has its own fill; Title and Description inset themselves a further --ui-space-xs, which is §6's rule encoded in the component rather than remembered at the call site.

do: Use ImageOverlay.Title and ImageOverlay.Description for caption text — they carry the only two inks measured against the veil.
Put actions in the `full` variant and captions in `scrim`; that is the difference between the two.
Pass alt="" when the picture is decoration and the caption already names the thing.
Reach for AspectRatio instead when there is nothing to put on top — an overlay with no children is a frame with a bar across it.
dont: Do not put arbitrary text on the veil with your own colour. --ui-text-inverse in particular is near-BLACK in the dark scheme, which is the mistake the sheet made and the reason --ui-text-on-media exists.
Do not weaken the veil to show more of the picture; its strength is the AA guarantee, not a taste setting.
Do not stack a second scrim inside — the guarantee is stated for one layer and two would be measured by nothing.
Do not rely on `[data-slot="aspect-ratio"]` to find the frame; the root replaces it with image-overlay.

a11y.role: none — a plain div. The inside carries the picture's semantics and its alt text.
a11y.name: The alt text names the picture. The caption is ordinary text in the reading order after it, so a screen reader gets the description and then the caption, rather than one string doing both jobs badly.
a11y.text: Title and Description are real paragraphs, not aria attributes, so they are selectable, translatable and reachable by a screen reader's normal reading order.
a11y.contrast: Text over a picture can only be guaranteed against the WORST picture, which is a white one. --ui-bg-media-floor is that case as an opaque role — the veil composited over white — and both inks are declared against it below, so check:contrast measures the guarantee in both schemes instead of a reviewer estimating it.

contrastPairs.role: the caption's first line, over the veil at its weakest possible reading
the caption's second line, same ground

forwarding.ref: Goes to the AspectRatio frame, which is the outermost node. ImageOverlay is not a form control, so the §5 default applies.
forwarding.className: Lands on the frame, so sizing, positioning or replacing the ratio all work exactly as they do on AspectRatio.
forwarding.rest: Native div props go to the frame. `data-slot` and `data-variant` are set by the component and a caller's would win — deliberately, since rest spreads last there.

needsDesign: The scrim's strength. The sheet ramps --ui-neutral-0 from 0% to 48%; over a white photograph that composites to a ground where the sheet's own inks measure 2.81:1 (title) and 2.11:1 (subtitle), both under AA. Shipped at 72%, where the SAME two inks measure 6.14:1 and 4.62:1. The drawing is otherwise unchanged. Confirm the darker veil, or confirm that captions are only ever placed over art-directed images and the guarantee should be dropped.

The sheet inks the caption with --ui-text-inverse and its second line with a raw --ui-neutral-80. Inverse is near-BLACK in the dark scheme, so the caption would have disappeared in dark only; neutral-80 is off the role layer entirely. Both are now --ui-text-on-media / --ui-text-on-media-muted, pinned to the same two values the sheet drew. No visual change in light.
The `full` variant is drawn as a 16%->48% ramp with its content CENTRED — i.e. the content sits where a ramp is weakest. Shipped as a flat veil at the same 72%, keeping the sheet's 8px blur. Confirm.
The second Image Overlay row is captioned 'Scrim' in the sheet; from the drawing it is the Full variant. Likely a copy/paste.

The `full` variant's action is drawn as a 1.5px --ui-border-subtle pill at 60% width with no fill — a bespoke control matching no Button variant, and one whose edge measures 4.62:1 against the veil in light and 2.02:1 in DARK. The veil deliberately does not follow the scheme and --ui-border-subtle does, so the same drawing drops its only boundary under the 3:1 non-text floor in one of them. Shipped as a slot instead, so the call site passes a real Button with its own fill. A button intended to sit on a photograph may be worth its own variant, and it would need an edge that does not follow the page either.
No hover, focus or pressed state is drawn, and an overlaid picture is very often a link. Nothing here is interactive.
knownGaps: Title and Description are clamped to one line each, which is what the sheet draws. A long asset name is truncated with no tooltip and no title attribute.
The veil is a single measured layer. Nesting a second one — a scrim inside a full — is not prevented and is not measured.
The `full` variant's backdrop blur is Tailwind's 8px step rather than a token; there is no blur scale in the contract, and one step is not a scale.
The AA guarantee covers this component's own two inks. Anything else placed on the veil — a consumer's own text, an icon — is measured by nothing.

contrast.role: the caption's first line, over the veil at its weakest possible reading
the caption's second line, same ground

changes.summary: Public library pages follow the manifest and typed documentation, with article-inspired copy and no changing library totals. Public leads and categories feed generated HTML references, Markdown twins, gallery and search entries, agent indexes and registry routes. The optional NetworkCanvas renderer now has its own typed reference. New freshness, source-boundary, route/link and browser checks keep the public reader in step. Interactive specimens are a featured subset; hosting and the remaining release gates stay open.

The four image-scrim roles are generalised into a MEDIA family and renamed: --ui-bg-scrim-image -> --ui-bg-media, --ui-bg-scrim-image-floor -> --ui-bg-media-floor, --ui-text-on-scrim -> --ui-text-on-media, --ui-text-on-scrim-muted -> --ui-text-on-media-muted. SCRIM_ALPHA -> MEDIA_SCRIM_ALPHA. Values are unchanged; only the names and the concept widen. The reason is a second use with the same requirement: an image editor's STAGE is the ground BEHIND a picture, where the overlay's veil is a scrim OVER one, and both need a neutral dark that follows neither the scheme nor the brand. The obvious alternative for a stage is --ui-bg-emphasis, which IS the accent — under a pale-yellow brand seed a photo editor's stage resolves to #ffe066 and every colour in the picture is judged against bright yellow. Keeping one role for both uses is what stops that being rediscovered, and --ui-bg-media-floor remains the right measurement target for both: ink on the full-strength opaque ground can only measure better than ink on the 72% veil.

migration.manual: Rename in place — no value changed. `--ui-bg-scrim-image` -> `--ui-bg-media` (utility `bg-scrim-image` -> `bg-media`), `--ui-bg-scrim-image-floor` -> `--ui-bg-media-floor`, `--ui-text-on-scrim` -> `--ui-text-on-media` (utility `text-ink-on-scrim` -> `text-ink-on-media`), `--ui-text-on-scrim-muted` -> `--ui-text-on-media-muted`. Importers of `SCRIM_ALPHA` take `MEDIA_SCRIM_ALPHA`. The roles shipped earlier the same day and no released consumer holds them.

changes.summary: A picture with content on top of it, in the sheet's two variants: `scrim` darkens the bottom edge and holds a caption, `full` covers the frame with an 8px backdrop blur and centres an action. It IS an AspectRatio frame rather than a copy of one, asserted as a relationship in the browser test. Three deviations from the sheet, each because the drawing does not survive a bright photograph: the veil is 72% rather than 48% (the sheet's own two inks measure 2.81:1 and 2.11:1 over white, and 6.14:1 / 4.62:1 at 72%); the caption's inks are --ui-text-on-scrim roles rather than --ui-text-inverse and a raw --ui-neutral-80; and the fade sits ABOVE the caption instead of behind it, because a single ramp under bottom-aligned text is under-strength for every line but the last. The `full` variant's veil is flat for the same reason — its content is centred, i.e. exactly where a ramp is weakest.

migration.manual: New item — nothing to migrate. `npx shadcn add @bydiorama/image-overlay`; it pulls in `cn` and `aspect-ratio`, and expects react as a peer.

items.name: image-upload
items.title: ImageUpload
items.lead: Adds images and explains the state of each upload.

docs.lead: Adds images and explains the state of each upload.
docs.name: ImageUpload
docs.summary: A form field whose control is a drop target. Four states — empty, busy, attached, rejected — plus a drag-over state the component owns itself. Built on a real <input type="file">, so the keyboard path is the native picker rather than a re-implementation. ImageUpload.File is one row mid-upload; ImageUpload.Grid and .Add are the multiple-image layout.

anatomy.notes: The field. Owns className and the ref, and carries data-status and data-dragging so a consumer or a test can see the state without reading classes.
A real <label> for the input. Input's label styling verbatim, so the two fields stack in a form without a seam.
The real <input type="file">, visually hidden. It is the field: accessible name, disabled state, accept, aria-invalid and aria-describedby all live here.
The 152px target. Owns the drag events and the outer edge, which is what changes on drag-over and on rejection.
The inner surface the prompt sits on. Washes to accent-subtle while a file is over the target.
The sentence, with the browse control inside it.
A real button that clicks the input. The keyboard path for everything the drop target offers a pointer.
role=status, so the upload announces itself to a screen reader that is not looking at it.
CSS, not an icon — griddy has no spinner glyph and check:icons forbids a private SVG. Suppressed under prefers-reduced-motion.
The rejection headline, on the danger well. Referenced by the input's aria-describedby.
The attached image slot. Takes an , an AspectRatio or an ImageOverlay.
Replace / Remove / Choose another file. A slot, so they are real Buttons at the call site.
The constraints. Turns danger-inked once one of them is broken, because they stop being guidance and become the reason.
ImageUpload.File — one row: thumb, name, a real Progress bar, detail and a cancel control.
ImageUpload.Grid — the framed well the tiles sit in. Same surface as the dropzone.
ImageUpload.Add — the 92px add tile, a real button.

docs.composition:
ImageUpload
├─ label        string (required)
├─ status?      "empty" | "busy" | "attached" | "rejected"
├─ errorText?   string — its PRESENCE is what makes the state "rejected"
├─ errorDetail? string
├─ helperText?  string
├─ prompt?      string   browseLabel?  string   busyText? string
├─ accept?      string   isMultiple?   boolean  isDisabled? boolean
├─ preview?     ReactNode — the attached image
├─ actions?     ReactNode — real Buttons
└─ onSelect?    (files: File[]) => void — fires for a drop AND for a browse

ImageUpload.File
├─ name         string (required)
├─ value?       number — omit once finished
├─ detail?      string   icon? ReactNode
└─ onCancel + cancelLabel — required together

ImageUpload.Grid   children: Thumbnail elements and an ImageUpload.Add
ImageUpload.Add    label (required)

label.notes: Required like every field here. A drop target with no name announces as a region and a file input with no name announces as 'browse' — neither says what is being uploaded.

status.notes: One closed union rather than three booleans, which would describe eight states of which five are nonsense. Drag-over is NOT in it: whether a file is currently over the target is something the component knows and a caller does not.

errorText.notes: Its presence puts the field in `rejected`, exactly as on Input — so a caller cannot show a message and forget the state, or set the state and forget the message. Wired to the input through aria-describedby and aria-invalid.

onSelect.notes: Fires for a drop AND for a browse, so a caller writes one path. Always an array, even when isMultiple is false.

preview.notes: The attached image. A slot rather than a src prop, so the caller decides between a bare , an AspectRatio and an ImageOverlay with a caption.

actions.notes: Replace / Remove / Choose another file. A slot, so they are real Buttons — the sheet draws them as bespoke pills whose edge measures 2.14:1.

isMultiple.notes: Native `multiple` on the input. The tile layout for several images is ImageUpload.Grid.

value.notes: ImageUpload.File only. Renders a real Progress at size xs. Omit it once the upload has finished and the bar disappears.

cancelLabel.notes: ImageUpload.File only, REQUIRED whenever onCancel is set. Name the file: five rows of 'Cancel' announce as five identical buttons.

do: Handle onSelect once — it fires for both the drop and the browse.
Pass the rejection reason as errorText and the remedy as errorDetail; the state follows the message.
Put real Buttons in `actions` — variant="outline" for Replace, "ghost" for Remove.
Name the file in cancelLabel, not just 'Cancel'.
dont: Do not set status="rejected" without errorText — errorText is what drives the state, so the two cannot disagree.
Do not re-implement the picker; the hidden input is the field, and clicking it from the browse button is the whole keyboard path.
Do not draw your own progress track in a file row — a hand-drawn one has no progressbar role and reaches for --ui-bg-accent, which measures 1.24:1 on the well.
Do not rely on the drag-over wash alone to signal a valid drop; the edge changes too, because a wash is colour only.

a11y.role: A native <input type="file"> with a real <label>. The drop target is a plain div — it is an addition, not the control.
a11y.name: The `label` prop, through htmlFor/id. The browse button carries its own name; the cancel control's is required by the type.

keyboard.does: Reaches the file input and the browse button — the picker is operable without a pointer at all.
Opens the native file picker from either. Native behaviour, not re-implemented.

a11y.status: The busy state is role=status, so an upload announces itself to a screen reader that is not watching the bar. The bar itself is a real Progress with aria-valuenow, named after the file.
a11y.error: errorText sets aria-invalid on the input and is referenced by aria-describedby. The rejection is carried by the BORDER, the icon, the message and the reddened helper — never by colour alone (1.4.1).

contrastPairs.role: the field label
the prompt, and the busy status — NOT the sheet's --ui-text-disabled, which measures 1.94:1 here
the browse control at rest
the browse control while a file is dragged over the target
the rejection headline and its detail, on the danger well
the helper once a constraint is broken
the helper at rest
a file row's name
a file row's detail, and its cancel glyph
the add tile's plus — a graphical control whose only visual channel is its glyph
the rejected dropzone's edge, which is the boundary that carries the state
the drag-over edge

contrastPairs.why: The resting dropzone edge, measured 1.47:1 light / 1.34:1 dark. Quiet by design (ADR 0010): the target is identified by its 152px well, its prompt and its icon, not by its hairline — and the two states where the edge DOES carry meaning (drag-over, rejected) are declared above at the 3:1 floor.

forwarding.ref: Goes to the outermost node rather than to the input, deliberately breaking §5's form-control rule: this field's control is visually hidden and a caller taking a ref wants the field, not the picker. The input is reachable through data-slot.
forwarding.className: Lands on the outermost node.
forwarding.rest: Native div props go to the outermost node; `accept`, `multiple` and `disabled` go to the input, which is the element that owns them.

needsDesign: The file row's progress fill is --ui-bg-accent, which measures 1.24:1 against its own track in light — the exact SC 1.4.11 failure --ui-bg-accent-legible was added to fix, and which Progress already ships. Shipped by reusing Progress, so the fill is 3.07:1. This is the fourth control to draw a value with the raw accent; the role exists.

The Replace / Choose another file pill is outlined in --ui-border-default, 2.14:1 light / 1.63:1 dark. That is the same finding already recorded against Button's outline variant, which now uses --ui-border-control at 3.11:1. Shipped as Button variant="outline" via the actions slot. Remove is Button variant="ghost".
The busy label is drawn in --ui-text-disabled, 1.94:1 light / 2.18:1 dark. It is live status, not a disabled control, and WCAG exempts the latter only. Shipped in --ui-text-secondary.

The rejection headline and detail are drawn in --ui-text-secondary and --ui-text-muted on the danger well; the detail measured 4.00:1 in dark on the old mid-grey ramp, under AA, and measures 5.27:1 on the 2026-11-03 warm-ink ramp. Shipped in --ui-text-on-danger-subtle, the role that exists for prose on a danger tint (8.52 / 9.53).

'browse' is drawn as styled text rather than a control, so the whole component was reachable by pointer only. Shipped as a real button, and underlined — a link identified by colour alone fails 1.4.1 independently of its contrast.
The field label is drawn at weight 550 while Input's is 500. Shipped at Input's, because two fields in one form should not have two label styles. Confirm which is the field-label weight.
No focus treatment is drawn for the dropzone, the browse control, the cancel control or the add tile. All four take the system focus ring.
No disabled state is drawn for any part.

The add tile has no drawn hover or pressed state, and the multiple row's helper says 'drag a tile to reorder' — a reorder the sheet does not otherwise draw, and which would need a keyboard path of its own (CardSorting's problem, and its solution).
The drag-over state is drawn only as valid. Nothing is drawn for a file being dragged over that will be REJECTED on drop, which is the moment the user can still act on it.
knownGaps: Reorder is not implemented. The sheet's helper mentions dragging a tile to reorder; that is CardSorting's job and would need the same keyboard path it has.
No client-side validation. The component does not read `accept` to reject a file — it reports what it is told through errorText. Deciding what is valid is the app's, since the limits are the app's.
The drag counter is a single boolean, so dragging over a child element and back out can flicker the wash on some browsers. It resolves on drop or on leaving the target.
ImageUpload.File does not truncate the middle of a long name; it truncates the end, so two files differing only in their extension look alike.
The busy state has no indeterminate form — ImageUpload.File without a `value` simply shows no bar.
docs.motion: The dropzone transitions `border-color` and `background-color` on drag-over; the browse and cancel controls transition `background-color` and `color`; all at --ui-duration-fast with --ui-ease-out. The busy spinner is a CSS keyframe under `motion-safe:`, and that variant — not the token layer — is what stops it under prefers-reduced-motion: `animate-spin` carries its own timing, so collapsing --ui-duration-* cannot reach it.

the prompt, and the busy status — NOT the sheet's --ui-text-disabled, which measures 1.94:1 here
the browse control at rest
the browse control while a file is dragged over the target
the rejection headline and its detail, on the danger well
the helper once a constraint is broken
the helper at rest
a file row's name
a file row's detail, and its cancel glyph
the add tile's plus — a graphical control whose only visual channel is its glyph
the rejected dropzone's edge, which is the boundary that carries the state
the drag-over edge
